GD01.title: One task at a time
GD01.chapter: Chapter 1 — The people still at the table

elements.text: April moved a stack of paper away from the edge of the table before Garrett could put another cup on it.
“I knew that was there,” he said.
“I know. I was worried about the cup.”
He looked at the space she had cleared. “You think I'm a mess.”
“I think you've started three things and finished none of them.”
“That's a system.”
“Then tell me which part I'm helping with.”
He almost said Charles. It would have been unfair, asking her to take a name and turn it into a task she could complete.
April waited. She had known him long enough to recognise the joke he was considering and long enough not to rescue him by laughing before he made it.
“I need to sort these,” he said at last. “The things I've actually checked. The things I keep going back to because I want them to be different.”
“Do you want me to read them?”
“Just the ones I hand you.”
“All right.”
She pulled a chair closer. He gave her a page, then took it back to look at the date again.
“You can keep that one for a moment,” she said.
“I know.”
“You don't have to do this quickly for me.”
That stopped him. He had been moving fast enough to pretend he knew what he was doing.
He passed her the page again and explained what he could actually verify. She asked questions without supplying the missing answers.
“Can we do something else first?” he asked. April closed the space between the piles without reading them. “Yes. Pick something small.”

His hand moved toward his phone before he remembered there was no new reason to check it. April noticed, but did not comment. The habit brought back a night when he had been unable to put it down at all.

GD02.title: When the calls stopped
GD02.chapter: Chapter 1 — The people still at the table

elements.text: FLASHBACK — Golden Dragon after closing, after Charles disappeared
The ringing had ended. Garrett kept the phone against his ear for another second, as though the silence might change its mind.
April set something on the table.
“How long have you been sitting here?”
“I checked work again.”
“That wasn't what I asked.”
“No one's heard anything.” He lowered the phone. “It rings. That's the worst part. It sounds like he could pick up.”
April sat opposite him. “Have you eaten?”
“I can't think about dinner.”
“Then don't. I brought something.”

He looked at the bowl and felt an unreasonable flash of irritation. There was food in the world, and people could still decide when to eat it, while he had lost the ability to make one conversation happen.
“I'm not hungry.”
“You don't have to finish it.”
“April.”
She left the bowl where it was. “I'm not trying to fix this with dinner.”
He looked away. “I know.”
For a while she let him be quiet.
“He made such a thing of coming home,” Garrett said. “Of telling someone where you were. He could turn it into a whole lecture.”
“You believed him.”
“I still do. That's the problem. I keep finding reasons it can't be his choice.”
“We don't know what happened.”
“What if he needed something? What if he called at the wrong time, or I missed something he said?”
April put both hands on the table, close to her own bowl.
“I can't answer that by inventing something you should have noticed.”
He swallowed. “First Mum and Dad. Then every time this goes quiet, I'm sixteen again.”
April's face changed, and he hated for a moment that she could see how frightened he was.
“You don't have to make that sound smaller with me,” she said.
“If I stop looking, even for tonight—”
He could not finish it without hearing how little sense it made.
“You'll still be his brother tomorrow,” she said. “We can write down who you've spoken to. What they actually know. We don't have to do all of it while you haven't eaten.”
“You can't promise he's coming back.”
“No.”
The honesty hurt. It also left him nothing he needed to argue against.
“Can you stay?”
“Yes.”
“Until I can put this down.”
April nodded. He turned the phone face down but kept it within reach. She did not ask him to move it farther away.
PRESENT DAY
He withdrew his hand from the phone and selected one page from the present pile. “This one,” he said quietly. He could begin with one thing that was true.

GD03.title: Dumpling inspection
GD03.chapter: Chapter 1 — The people still at the table

elements.text: Rei had barely sat down before Garrett pointed at the plate.
“No formal assessment tonight.”
“I haven't seen it yet.”
“You're familiar with my work.”
“That's why I came.”
Garrett had a reply ready, then found he did not want to use it. He set the plate down more carefully than necessary.
Rei glanced at the dumplings. “This one's uneven.”
“And yet you survived the first.”
“It had character.”
Garrett laughed. “You cannot keep saying that as though it makes you less difficult.”
Rei looked amused, unhurried. He did not fill the space by asking immediately whether there was news. Garrett realised he had begun bracing for that question whenever someone cared enough to visit.
“Do you remember what I thought you were doing?” he asked.
“Complaining.”
“You were drawing an injured dumpling on the receipt.”
“Split.”
“An important distinction to the dumpling.”
The argument was familiar enough to be comfortable. Beneath it, Garrett remembered the stranger with the sketchbook, and how unexpectedly pleased he had been when that stranger came back.

GD04.title: The split dumpling
GD04.chapter: Chapter 1 — The people still at the table

elements.text: FLASHBACK — Golden Dragon, early months
Rei had come in alone after a modelling shoot, a sketchbook resting against his leg. Garrett noticed the opened seam before he put the plate down. An imperfect plate was something he could fix.
“Give me that one. I’ll replace it.”
“It’s all right.”
“It’s opened.”
“I can see that.”
Rei pulled the receipt closer and drew the crooked seam. When Garrett returned, he glanced at the paper.
“Is that a complaint?”
“It has more character than the intact ones.”
“That sounds suspiciously like a polite complaint.”
“I ate it.”
“A committed critic.”
The answer surprised Garrett into a smile. Here was a customer taking the care he had put into the meal seriously, without asking him to apologise for its seam.
“Can I keep that?”
“What for?”
“To remember the standard I’m being held to.”
“It isn’t a standard.”
“Good. I was worried I’d have to break one on every plate.”
Rei pushed the receipt toward him. Garrett pinned it up and straightened it. He wanted to keep this small encounter somewhere he could see it.
“You don’t have to display it.”
“I know.”
Rei finished his meal slowly. Garrett returned to work and remembered the order.
PRESENT DAY
Rei was looking at him over the current plate.
“What?” Garrett asked.
“You stopped talking.”
“Rare event. You should appreciate it.”
“I was.”
Garrett leaned against the nearest available surface. “Can you stay a while?”
Rei nodded. Garrett did not need to attach a search update to the invitation.

GD05.title: A lead small enough to doubt
GD05.chapter: Chapter 1 — The people still at the table

elements.text: Mei turned the old dispatch photograph so Garrett could see the correction.
“Six to four,” she said. “Here.”
He saw the number, then the letter beside it. The crooked H reached him before he had decided what he was looking for.

Charles used to leave notes on the fridge. Garrett remembered being annoyed by how often they contained something he already knew: food, a time, something to remember before going out. Now a shape in a photograph made his chest tighten.
“That's his writing.”
Mei did not agree quickly enough.
“It looks like it,” Garrett corrected himself.
“I thought you should see it.”
“Why didn't—” He stopped. “Sorry. I don't mean that.”
She left the photograph between them.
The date was eleven days after Charles had left his job. Garrett checked it again, trying not to build a journey out of one correction.
“If it's him, he was doing something ordinary,” he said. “Changing a number.”
“It tells us somebody corrected the count.”
“I know what it tells us.” His voice had sharpened. He took a breath. “I know. I'm trying to get the rest of me to keep up.”
Mei nodded. He was grateful she did not ask him to be calmer before continuing.
“The stamp's cut off,” he said.
“There is a complete receiving copy.”
He looked at the photograph once more. The resemblance did not become proof because it hurt to leave it uncertain.

GD06.title: Mei remembers the working day
GD06.chapter: Chapter 2 — What a record can prove

elements.text: Garrett took a stack of clean things from Mei when she indicated where they belonged. He needed something to do with his hands while she found the copy.
“Is that helping,” she asked, “or are you going to move everything back afterward?”
“I can do useful work while waiting.”
“Good. Put those there.”
He did. When she laid the record down, he nearly abandoned the last item halfway to its place. He finished moving it first.
The full stamp named West Pier Cold Storage in Hong Kong. Four crates received. No driver signature.
Garrett looked at the space where a name might have been.
“You don't remember who took them?”
“Not enough to give you a name.”
“A description?”
“I don't want to give you something you'll spend a week trying to turn into Charles.”
He looked up, stung, then saw how carefully she was choosing the words.
“You think I'd do that.”
“I think you're hoping. I would rather disappoint you honestly than send you after a person I can't remember.”
He pressed his lips together. “All right.”
Mei pointed out what the receiving record could support. Garrett followed the dates and copied the details he was entitled to keep.
“Thank you,” he said afterward.
“For the paper?”
“For not saying you remember when you don't.”
He went back to the item he had almost dropped. The next place to look was the duplicate tally, not an imagined driver with his brother's face.

GD07.title: What the records cannot say
GD07.chapter: Chapter 2 — What a record can prove

elements.text: Two crates had remained at dispatch.
Garrett read the tally again. Six packed, four collected. The correction accounted for the difference. It did not hide a passenger in the arithmetic.
He had not realised how much of a story he had attached to the missing two until the paper took it away.
“Four,” he said under his breath.
An entirely sensible number. He disliked it for a moment.

He pictured Charles looking over his shoulder and telling him to read what was actually there. Then he was angry that he could imagine his brother correcting him more readily than answering the phone.
Garrett moved his notes apart. On one side, the date and delivery acceptance. On the other, the question of who had authorised collection.
He wrote the two quantities beside their actual labels. It felt pedantic until he saw how easily he had been treating them as the same thing.
He wrote that the discrepancy proved neither Charles's authorship nor his travel. He left room for the answer to arrive later instead of forcing one into the line.
He did not have to feel pleased with the correction for it to be useful. Someone had still ordered the collection. Finding out who was a question a record might answer.
When he stood, the disappointment went with him. So did the next question.

GD08.title: A question worth asking
GD08.chapter: Chapter 2 — What a record can prove

elements.text: Dana let Garrett finish explaining before she moved the receiving record closer.
“This establishes delivery acceptance,” she said.
“And the date.”
“Yes.”
“But not who went with it.”
“Not from this record.”
He looked at the stamp. “I keep bringing people something that almost answers me.”
Dana paused. “It may help to make the next question smaller.”
“My brother is missing. It's not a small question.”
“No. But this document cannot answer all of it.”
He leaned back, hearing the impatience in his own voice too late.
“Sorry.”
“You can ask about the dispatch authorisation. Who ordered the collection, on what date, under which reference.”
“And if his name is there?”
“Then you have the information the authorisation actually records. You check it against the other material.”
He gave a short laugh without much humour. “You don't leave a lot of room to jump ahead.”
“I'm trying to give you somewhere you can step.”
Garrett looked at her properly. She had not promised an investigation, private access or a result. She had listened and given him a question he could use.
“Show me how to request it,” Garrett said.

He wrote down the requirement for a dated authorisation. The public desk remained a public desk. Leaving with something limited and usable felt better than leaving with a reassurance he could not test.

GD09.title: Dinner without a report
GD09.chapter: Chapter 2 — What a record can prove

elements.text: April took one look at the papers beside Garrett's plate.
“Are those eating with us?”
He moved them. “They don't order much.”
“They occupy a lot of table.”
He put them away, then began to explain the tally.
April waited until he noticed she had not asked.
“You don't want to hear it?”
“I will, if you want to tell me. I also came to have dinner with you.”
He looked down at the food. “I don't know what else I've got to say.”
“You could ask me something.”
That embarrassed him more than a rebuke would have.
“How was your day?”
“Do you want the version where I say fine and we go back to your papers?”
“No.” He put his hands flat beside the plate. “The actual version.”
April studied him, then smiled a little. “I wanted an evening that wasn't organised around fixing something.”
“And I started with freight records.”
“You did.”
“I can be charming without a document.”
“I remember. That's why I keep trying this.”

He laughed. She asked him to pass something, and for a while they discussed the meal, something ordinary he had done badly and something he thought he had done very well. She did not agree with his assessment of the second.
Later, when his attention drifted, she touched the edge of the table rather than his papers.
“Still here?”
“Trying.”
“That's enough. You don't need to be entertaining for two people.”
He took another bite before answering. He wanted her to have an evening with him in it, not just a place beside his search.

GD10.title: The page that is not there

elements.text: Mei had the index ready. Garrett recognised the reference before she pointed to it.
“That matches.”
“Yes.”
“Where's the authorisation?”
“Missing from this set.”
He shut his eyes briefly. “Of course it is.”
“Garrett.”
“I know. It's not your fault.”
He had answered the reassurance before she offered it. She waited until he looked at her again.
“The former records custodian may have the retained copy.”
“May.”
“Yes.”
He looked at the index. The absence was so ordinary it was almost insulting: a page not where it belonged, after all the hope he had carried into the room.
“Can we request it?”
“We can send the matching reference.”
He read it aloud carefully. He would rather spend another minute making sure the number was right than spend tomorrow wondering whether he had hurried the one part he could control.
When it was done, Garrett remained by the table.
“That's all for today?”
“For this request.”
He nodded. The distinction gave him somewhere to put the rest of the day. Waiting for a response was an action with a limit, not permission to sit here until the paper arrived.
The retained page was waiting when the next response arrived. Garrett started with the date, then the crate count, then the reference.
The agreement between the fields made him want to move faster. He deliberately read the next line twice.
Greyglass Service House. Winterfield.
A place he could approach. Something close enough that his mind immediately tried to put Charles inside it.
He caught himself tracing a route before he had finished reading what the place was named as: equipment-service correspondent.
Not passenger. Not destination of a missing man.

Garrett checked the date, crate count and reference number, then recorded the supported connection. “What work was this account handling?” was a question he could ask without beginning with an accusation.

The name alone did not establish the connection. Garrett read the same page after the correction and felt foolish, then angry about feeling foolish. He could wait for tomorrow and ask the narrower question. He could not make a failed enquiry advance by wanting it enough.
When he finally left with a verified reference, it was smaller than the story he had almost told himself. It was also something that would still be true when he got there.
“A quiet martial artist,” the clerk said.
Garrett's first response was recognition. His second was the knowledge that he had not been shown a person, only a description broad enough to fit one he missed.
“What do you mean by quiet?”
“Didn't say much while checking the returned equipment.”
“Did he give a name?”
“Not one I can confirm for you from that recollection.”
Garrett shifted his weight. The clerk's restraint began to sound like obstruction because he wanted it to be concealing a useful answer.
“Can I see the dated service receipt?”
The available record connected the consignment to a private research-office account. It did not put a face beside the recollection.
“Could a family enquiry go through the return-document channel?” Garrett asked.
The clerk agreed to accept a sealed enquiry through the existing channel. Garrett sat with the blank paper longer than he expected.
What did he write to someone who might not be his brother? What did he write if it was?
He kept the question private and direct. He did not demand that a stranger open it and prove care on his behalf.
“You're hiding him.” The words arrived before Garrett had decided to say them.
The clerk drew the papers back to their own side. “That isn't what these records establish.”
Garrett heard himself preparing another accusation and stopped. The clerk would not answer it. He would have to wait until tomorrow and return to the document request.
The enquiry was sent, not answered. He had placed a question where it might reach Charles without pretending that delivery guaranteed a reply.
The returned reference mentioned blue and red research files.

Garrett read it beside the street rumour. The rumour had an answer for every missing part. Everyone associated with the office became a dealer. Every unexplained movement became evidence of the same thing.
He could see why it travelled more easily than a careful sentence full of limits.

He compared the references across the retained copies. They were consistent. The labels did not establish what Charles sold, whether he had been abducted, or why he had left. His sealed enquiry had reached the office. That was the actual change.
He pictured repeating the rumour to April or Rei and hearing it become more convincing in his own voice. He put it aside before that happened.

He had written a rumour as though it were an answer. The enquiry paused. The accusation produced no confession; the notes still distinguished what he had chosen to claim from what anyone had verified.

For a moment he was angry with Charles for making him do this: separate paper from hope, hope from suspicion, suspicion from things he would hate to have said if his brother walked through the door tomorrow.
Then he folded the verified reference carefully. Anger was something he could admit. It did not need a false charge attached to it.

GD14.title: What you know, what you hope

elements.text: “I keep doing it,” Garrett said.
Rei waited.
“Getting halfway to an answer and finishing it myself.”
“Do you want to tell me which part?”
Garrett selected only what he was willing to share. He left private recipients and unverified allegations out of it.
“When I get something useful, I think the next thing has to be useful too. Then if it isn't, I feel like somebody's taken it away.”
Rei looked at the cleared space between them. “What did you have before you looked?”
“Don't do that.”
“What?”
“Ask a sensible question while I'm trying to be unreasonable.”
Rei's mouth curved slightly. “You could warn me.”
Garrett laughed, then rubbed a hand over his face.
“I had a possibility.”
“Do you still have one?”
“Yes. Just not the one I spent an hour imagining.”
Rei nodded. He did not tell Garrett to stop imagining things, which would have made him feel less understood.
“Sometimes I don't want to tell anyone about a lead,” Garrett said. “Because if it goes nowhere, I have to watch them be disappointed for me.”
“I can let you tell me when you know what it means.”
“And before?”
“Before too. If you tell me you're not sure.”
Garrett looked at him. “You make that sound very undramatic.”
“I thought you could supply that part.”
The laugh came more easily this time. Garrett stood to finish the washing. Rei stayed and took the drying cloth without being asked.
The familiar division of washing and drying recalled how it had developed. For Garrett, it began with remembering an order, then noticing when Rei came without one.
FLASHBACK — Subsequent Golden Dragon visits
Garrett remembered Rei's order the next time and was pleased by the small pause before Rei answered. It was possible to get something right without making a performance of it.

On later visits, Garrett asked about the sketchbook. Rei explained what he was trying to make. Garrett caught himself reaching for a clever comment before the explanation was finished and let him finish instead.
Another evening, Rei picked up a cloth while Garrett washed bowls.
“You don't have to do that.”
“I know.”
Garrett slid a bowl within reach.

The silence that followed made him restless at first. He nearly asked whether something was wrong. Instead he told Rei about a kitchen problem because it was what he had actually been thinking about. Rei listened, then offered an opinion that Garrett disputed for the pleasure of the argument.
The work finished without either of them having had to explain why company helped.
Later still, Rei came in without looking toward the menu.
“Food?” Garrett asked.
“No. I just—”
Garrett pulled out a chair.
“All right. Sit down.”
He tried not to make it sound like he had been hoping for this exact thing: someone arriving because the room contained him, rather than because he could provide a meal or an answer.
PRESENT DAY
Rei finished drying the bowl Garrett had passed him.
“You don't have to stay because I'm waiting for something,” Garrett said.
“I know.”
It was the same answer. Garrett understood it better now. He let the next silence happen without arranging a reason for either of them to fill it.

GD16.title: A question only family can answer
GD16.chapter: Chapter 4 — A question only family can answer

elements.text: The handwritten reply contained a question.
When we tried to make her broth again, what did we use to measure it?
Garrett read it once as a test and once as something that had happened to him.

There was no phone number. No open declaration that would make the rest of the search unnecessary. Whoever had written it was asking him to reach into a part of his life the papers had never contained.
For a moment he resented that too. He had come this far and was still being asked to prove something.
Then he remembered the kitchen, the effort of trying to make a familiar taste arrive through ingredients neither brother trusted himself to measure correctly.

The reply could not authenticate him. “No,” Garrett said, too late to make the sent answer different. Certainty said loudly would not repair it. He would have to wait until the next story day to answer again.

The reply answered with the unfinished shrimp-shell argument from their last call. A private evening invitation followed: the Glasshouse, between seven and eleven, alone. Garrett unfolded the visitor directions, then returned to the question that had made them possible.

GD17.title: The chipped teacup
GD17.chapter: Chapter 4 — A question only family can answer

elements.text: FLASHBACK — An earlier attempt to recreate their mother's broth
Charles looked at the chipped cup in Garrett's hand.
“You could use something easier to measure with.”
“I'm measuring with it.”
“That's not the same thing.”
“It is if I keep using the same one.”
Charles gave him the look that usually meant the argument had become more work than doing it himself. Garrett held onto the cup.
“I've got this part.”
“All right.”
The concession surprised him enough that he nearly spilled it anyway.
They tasted what they had made and looked away from each other at almost the same time.
“Not quite,” Charles said.
“You don't have to make it sound like a school report.”
“What would you like me to say?”
“That it tastes wrong.”
Charles put down the spoon. “It tastes wrong.”
Garrett had asked for the words. Hearing them made his eyes sting.
He busied himself with the cup.
“I thought I'd know,” he said. “Once it was there. I thought I'd be able to tell what was missing.”
Charles leaned against the counter. “I thought I would too.”
For a while neither tried to fix the recipe.
Garrett turned the cup until the chip faced away from his thumb. “I remember her making it look easy.”
“I don't think we were paying attention to the difficult parts.”
“We were paying attention to eating it.”
Charles's mouth moved into a tired smile. “You were very committed.”
Garrett laughed, then had to wipe at his face. He did not like doing both at once.
“Don't throw it out,” he said when Charles reached for the pot.
“I wasn't going to.”
“We can still eat it.”
“Yes.”
“And try again.”
Charles nodded. Garrett left their father's cup beside the other things, without announcing why he wanted it there.
PRESENT DAY

He could remember wanting the broth right without pretending he remembered a complete recipe. The authenticated reply's ordinary disagreement belonged to the same relationship. A family memory was suddenly being answered by someone alive.
The memory came back with no new reply attached to it. He had answered the enquiry incorrectly. Remembering the cup now would not send another answer or bring tomorrow closer.

GD18.title: Until the door
GD18.chapter: Chapter 4 — A question only family can answer

elements.text: “I thought you'd look happier,” April said, then shook her head. “Sorry. That isn't fair.”
“I thought I would too.”
He had checked the permitted time again before coming to see her. Nineteen hundred to twenty-three hundred. The numbers were easier to hold than the possibility of Charles's face.
“Have you decided what you're going to say?”
“Yes.”
She waited.
“About six different things.”
“Do they all fit together?”
“No.”
April smiled briefly, then looked at his hands.
“I want to ask you to be careful,” she said. “And I don't want it to sound like I'm asking you not to want this.”
“I know.”
“Do you?”
He looked up. “Yes. I'm just not very good at having room for anything else right now.”
“Then let's agree on something small. Do you want to let me know when you're able afterward?”
“I might not know what to say.”
“You can say that.”
“And if I don't want to talk?”
“Then don't agree to a conversation. Agree to whatever you can actually do.”
He considered it instead of promising the answer that would end her worry fastest.
They agree on a limited check-in without operational details.
“I can't promise tonight.” April nods. “Then I won't pretend you did. You can find me when you're ready.”
Before he leaves, Garrett says, “Thank you for not telling me how I ought to feel.”
April gives him a small, crooked smile. “I started badly.”
“You came back.”

GD19.title: You can ask me to stay
GD19.chapter: Chapter 4 — A question only family can answer

elements.text: “I keep thinking I'm going to see him and forget every question,” Garrett said.
Rei was quiet for a moment. “Which one matters most?”
“All of them.”
“I thought you might say that.”
Garrett looked toward the door. “Why didn't you call? Where were you? Did you know what you were doing to me? Are you all right?” He stopped. “That last one keeps getting in front of the others.”
“It doesn't make the others disappear.”
“No. It just makes me feel terrible for having them.”
Rei leaned forward. “You can be glad to see someone and still have something to ask them.”
“You sound prepared.”
“I'm sitting here. You're the one who has to go.”
Garrett looked at him properly. The admission made the advice easier to hear.
“I have to go alone,” he said.
“All right.”
“You're not going to offer anyway?”
“Would that help?”
“No.” He laughed softly. “I was ready to argue with you about it.”
“I could find something else.”
Garrett's shoulders lowered. “Can you stay until I need to leave?”
“Yes.”
They did not rehearse the whole conversation. Garrett tried one opening, hated it and abandoned it. Rei made no effort to turn it into a polished speech.
Garrett was still frightened when the conversation ended. He was also no longer alone with every version of the meeting he had imagined.

GD20.title: Before the laboratory door
GD20.chapter: Chapter 5 — The brother behind the door

elements.text: Garrett had rehearsed enough sentences to fill the corridor. At the door he could remember only fragments.
I thought you were dead.
Don't tell me to calm down.
Are you hurt?
He disliked that the last question could still undo the first two. He wanted to be angry without losing the part of himself that would reach for Charles if he needed help.
He looked at the permission that had brought him this far. A private visit, not faction clearance. An evening window, not an explanation.
He remembered another doorway: school gates, Charles waiting, both of them convinced that fear entitled them to tell the other what to do.

GD21.title: An older brother's responsibility
GD21.chapter: Chapter 5 — The brother behind the door

elements.text: FLASHBACK — Hong Kong, Garrett aged sixteen
Charles was waiting outside the school.
Garrett slowed, then deliberately made his pace casual.
“You came all the way here to glare at me?”
“I came because every school in the district seems to know your name.”
“So you've heard.” Garrett tried to keep the pride out of his voice and failed. “They're together now. They're not fighting each other.”
“You beat people until they agreed to follow you.”
“They respect me.”
“Some of them fear you.”
Garrett looked away. “You don't know them.”
“I know the difference.”
“Then stop talking to me like I'm stupid.”
He tried to push past. Charles caught his arm. What happened next was too quick for Garrett's anger to prepare him: Charles struck him, knocked him down and hit him again before stopping.
For a moment Garrett could hear his own breathing more clearly than anything Charles said.
Charles stepped back. Garrett got to his knees without taking the offered hand.
“Is that it?” Garrett asked. “Is that how you teach me not to fight?”
Charles's hand lowered.
“No.”
“You called me a delinquent. What does that make you?”
“Your brother. Who just hurt you.” Charles swallowed. “I was wrong.”
Garrett looked at him, too angry to decide what to do with the admission.
“You sound like you hate me.”
“I am terrified of losing you.”
“Then say that before you hit me.”
“Yes.” Charles's voice was rougher now. “That is what I should have done.”
The pavement between them seemed much larger than it had before.
“Since Mum and Dad died, I keep thinking I have to know how to do everything,” Charles said. “Food. School. You coming home. And when I don't know, I make another rule.”
“I lost them too.”
“I know.”
“No. You know it happened to me. You keep acting like what I'm supposed to do about it is obey you.”
Charles looked down. He did not answer quickly.
Garrett sat back, breathing hard. “I thought if I got strong enough, no one could take anything else.”
“So did I,” Charles said. “Strength doesn't make that promise true.”
“What am I meant to do with everyone following me?”
“Be responsible for what you ask of them.”
“They stopped fighting each other.”
“Then keep them safe. No making children prove themselves. No threatening families or shopkeepers. If somebody wants out, let them go.”
“And if they think I'm weak?”
“Take the insult.” Charles paused. “An older brother carries responsibility, not ownership. A leader should learn the same thing.”
Garrett looked directly at him. “You have to learn it too.”
“Yes. Starting with you. I'm sorry.”
The apology did not take away the ache or the humiliation. It made Charles responsible for doing something different after this.
“I miss them,” Garrett said.
“Every day.”
After a while, Garrett let him sit beside him.
“Will you come home tonight?”
“With you. And we'll get that bruise looked at.”
They left together. Garrett did not have to call what happened right in order to want his brother beside him.
PRESENT DAY
Adult Garrett stood at the laboratory approach. Being strong enough to arrive did not make him less in need of an answer. The door in front of him belonged to the present.

GD22.title: The reunion, before the fight
GD22.chapter: Chapter 5 — The brother behind the door

elements.text: Charles was standing in front of him.

Garrett had imagined this often enough that he distrusted the first second of it. He looked for something ordinary to confirm it: the angle of Charles's shoulders, the way he went still before choosing what to say.
“You're here,” Garrett said.
“Yes.”
The answer was so small that Garrett almost laughed.
“That's it?”
Charles glanced at the door. “Keep your voice down.”
For months, Garrett had wanted nothing more than to hear that voice. Now he could barely stand it.
“Don't do that.”
“Garrett—”
“Don't start with an instruction. You don't get to disappear and have the first thing you say be something I'm doing wrong.”
Charles looked back at him. “You're right.”
Garrett had been ready for an argument. The admission left him with nowhere to put the next sentence.
“I called you.”
“I know.”
“How much do you know? Do you know I kept thinking there must be some reason you couldn't pick up? Not wouldn't. Couldn't.”
Charles's hands shifted at his sides, then stopped.
“I thought keeping you away from this would keep you safe.”
“You keep saying safe like it tells me where you were.”
“I can't explain this in a corridor.”
“Then explain it here. I'm here.” Garrett spread his hands, angry at how much they were shaking. “You can see that, can't you? I'm not a voice on your phone anymore.”
Charles took a breath. “There are people who could use you to get to me.”
“So you made sure I couldn't get to you either.”
“I was afraid.”
Garrett looked at him. For a moment it was easier to be furious than to hear that.
“So was I,” he said. “Every day. You left me with that, and you weren't even there to be angry at.”
Charles lowered his gaze, briefly.
“I didn't know how to tell you enough without bringing you into it.”
“You could have told me you were alive.”
The words came out quieter than Garrett expected. They hurt more that way.
“I needed my brother,” he said. “I didn't need you to have every answer. I needed you to let me know you were still somewhere in the world.”
Charles looked up again. “I am.”
“I can see that now.” Garrett swallowed. “You don't understand how long it took me to get to now.”
Charles looked toward the door as though it still offered an answer.
“You shouldn't be here.”
Garrett felt the admission of fear vanish behind another instruction.
“Where should I be? At home, calling you again?”
“Somewhere they can't use you.”
“Who?”
“I can't bring you into this.”
“You brought me into the part where I didn't know whether you were alive.”
Charles's expression tightened. “Hate me if you have to. I wanted you to live.”
“Stop saying it like I had to lose you to do that.”
Silence settled between them. Garrett could see the effort Charles was making to remain controlled, and for once he did not want to make that easier for him.
“I needed you,” he said. “You decided I could manage without you, and you didn't even ask.”
“I am not coming back into your life. Go home.”
The refusal landed harder because Charles was standing so close.
Garrett took a breath. “Look at me.”
“I am.”
“Not at the kid you remember. At me.”
Charles's hands shifted. “You fought your way this far. That doesn't mean you understand what's waiting here.”
“No. It means you don't get to call me helpless because trusting me is frightening.”
“If you cannot get past me, you cannot survive what comes after me.”
His voice caught on the last words. He covered it by raising his hands.
Garrett felt his own anger harden into something he could act on. He also recognised the old mistake taking shape between them: deciding that force could finish an argument fear had started.
“You want to make me leave?”
“If that is what it takes.”
“Then fight me. And when I'm still standing, you listen.”

GD23.title: What he can finally say
GD23.chapter: Chapter 5 — The brother behind the door

elements.text: For a moment Garrett could think only about getting his breathing under control.
Charles did not tell him to leave again.
“Are you going to listen?” Garrett asked.
“Yes.”
The answer made him want to sit down more than any blow had.
“You don't have to carry my safety alone.”
Charles looked at him. “I thought keeping you out of it would keep you safe.”
“It left me searching.”
“I know.”
“Say it like you know what I was searching for.”
Charles lowered his gaze to the file he was holding, then set it down.
“Your brother.”
Garrett pressed his lips together and waited.
“I came here deliberately,” Charles said. “Sylvanis thinks I work for him. I needed to get close enough to understand what happened to our parents.”

The explanation did not arrive in the order Garrett wanted. Alive. Deliberate. Undercover. Their parents. Each word changed the shape of something he had feared without answering every question inside it.
“You chose to disappear.”
“Yes.”
“Do you know who did it?”
“I don't have proof against a named killer to give you.”
Garrett looked away. Part of him had wanted the explanation to include a target, something clear enough to hold all the anger that no longer knew where to go.
Charles continued more quietly. “I wanted an answer. I made you live inside another unanswered question while I looked.”
“You should have trusted me with the choice.” Charles does not argue.
“I needed my brother, not another mystery.” Charles answers, “I know,” without supplying an efficient correction.
Only now does Charles share his private number for direct texts. Garrett looks at it for longer than entering it requires.
“You'll answer?”
“When I can do so safely. And I will tell you when I can't.”
The number is not a public contact, a group-chat invitation or a release from the laboratory. Charles remains here. Garrett has found him, and that is different from bringing him home.

GD24.title: Choose what comes next
GD24.chapter: Chapter 5 — The brother behind the door

elements.text: Garrett had imagined an ending that would make it impossible to be angry anymore. Standing beside Charles, he understood how unreasonable that had been.
“I won't expose you,” he said.
Charles nodded.
“Don't nod like the difficult part is over.”
“I don't think it is.”
“Then write. Even if all you can say is that you're still here.”
“I can do that.”
“And don't make me earn every ordinary thing by finding the right document.”
Charles looked down briefly. “You shouldn't have had to.”
Garrett let the admission stand. “I want to keep talking to you. That's not the same as saying none of it hurt.”
“I understand.”
“Keep understanding when I bring it up again.”
Charles gave him a tired, faint smile. “I will try to do better than defend myself.”
“I won't expose you,” Garrett repeated. “That doesn't make the silence all right.”
“No.”
“I can't promise to be easy about this because I know why now.”
“I'm not asking you to forgive me tonight.”
“You were asking me to go home a few minutes ago. Give me time to believe the new answer.”
Charles accepted that without correcting the chronology or the tone.
“Then I will keep the agreement while you decide what you can trust.”

GD25.title: The chair at the table
GD25.chapter: Chapter 5 — The brother behind the door

elements.text: Garrett put out two bowls.
He noticed what he had done while reaching for the second spoon.
Charles was alive. Charles was staying at the laboratory. These facts belonged in the same evening, although his hands had apparently accepted only the first.
He set the spoon down.
The recipe book lay beside the Red Dragons accounts. He had carried two kinds of unfinished work home and expected one of them to feel like relief.

For a moment he wanted to call Charles just to hear him answer. Then he remembered the agreement about when he could safely speak. The distinction between caution and disappearance would have to be learned through actual replies, not settled by one frightened test tonight.

Garrett left the second bowl within reach but did not wait for someone to fill the chair before he ate. It could mean there was a place when Charles could visit. It did not have to mean every meal was unfinished without him.
He carried it back carefully. Putting it away felt harsher than he intended until he remembered that he could take it out again. He was arranging tonight's table, not sentencing the relationship.
He opened the recipe book. His parents were still gone. Charles's mission remained incomplete. The people who came to him tomorrow would still need something he could actually do.
He could not cook the missing years back into the room. He could make food for the person who was here.

GD26.title: You do not owe me the whole story

elements.text: April did not begin by asking where he had been.
“You came,” she said.
“If we agreed to talk, I should probably turn up.”
“If we agreed,” she corrected gently. “Don't borrow a promise you didn't make.”
Garrett sat down. He had expected the first conversation afterward to be easy because he finally had something better than uncertainty to offer.
“He's alive.”
April's expression changed before she spoke. “You know?”
“Yes. I've seen him.”
She let out a breath. Garrett looked at her hands and realised she had been holding some of this worry without asking him to carry it for her.
“I can't tell you everything,” he said.
“All right.”
“I hate saying that to you.”
“Then tell me what you can. Or tell me how you are.”
“I don't know how to be relieved without being furious.”
“You don't have to pick one for my benefit.”
He looked down. “You wanted him back too.”
“I wanted you to have an answer. I didn't decide what the answer was allowed to do to you.”
“Something changed. I can't explain it yet.”
April waited, then nodded. “Do you want company with that, or somewhere to put it down for a while?”
“You don't mind not knowing?”
“I mind that it's difficult for you. That's different from being owed the details.”

He asked about her evening before it became another conversation entirely arranged around his needs. She answered, then asked him to stay for part of it. The invitation was something ordinary they could both choose.
Rei listened without interrupting. When Garrett finished saying Charles was alive, he looked down at the table for a moment.
“I'm glad,” he said.
Garrett nodded. “Me too.”
“But?”
“I don't want there to be a but.”
Rei waited.
“I have things I want to say to him that don't sound like being glad.”
“Then don't say all of them to me instead.”
Garrett looked up, surprised.
“I'll listen,” Rei added. “But if there's something he needs to hear, being polite here won't tell him.”
“I wasn't planning to be polite.”
“You were trying to apologise for being angry before you said anything.”
Garrett gave a short laugh. “That's irritatingly observant.”
“I've had practice with you.”
For a while they were quiet.
“He's still my brother,” Garrett said.
“Yes.”
“I keep saying that like it tells me what to do.”
“What do you want to do next?”
“Talk again. Not tonight. And not pretend we don't need to.”
Rei nodded. “That sounds like something you can tell him.”

“I have an answer I can’t share yet,” Garrett said.

“Then I won’t guess it for you.” Rei moved his cup aside. “Company, or a change of subject?”

“Company. We can find the subject after.”
Garrett asked about Rei’s day and waited for the answer. There was room at the table for something that had happened to someone else.
The shopkeeper laid two demands on the table. Garrett saw the rival names before he saw the amounts, and made himself read the rest.
A runner beside him spoke first.
“We could make this disappear. If the street pays us instead—”
“No,” Garrett said.
The runner looked at him, startled by how quickly the answer came.
“We'd be keeping them safe.”
“If they have to buy our kindness, we've only changed the name on the threat.”
The shopkeeper did not look reassured yet. Garrett noticed and stopped preparing the next impressive sentence.
“What?” he asked.
“If one of your people says that when you're not here, who do I tell?”
“Me.”
“And if the person I have to get past to reach you is wearing the same colours?”
Garrett felt the question land in the silence around the table.
Mei spoke carefully. “They need something they can use when this conversation is over.”
The runner shifted. “You're making it sound as though we're the same as them.”
The shopkeeper looked at him. “I asked what happens if you're the one at my door.”
Garrett held up a hand before the answer could become an argument about respect.
“You don't have to reassure us while asking for help.”
He looked at the runner. “No protection fees. No forced recruitment. No punishment for a complaint or for refusing an escort.”
“What am I supposed to do?”
“For now, no civilian-facing work while this is reviewed.”
Garrett turned back to the shopkeeper.
“There will be a way to report it without asking that person's permission. We'll explain how it works, not just give it a name.”
“People who aren't answerable to our rank need a place in reviewing complaints. You shouldn't have to join us to be heard.”
“Do I have to decide about an escort now?” the shopkeeper asked.
“No,” Garrett said. “You can say no.”
He waited while they considered it. Letting the answer take time was the first thing he could do to make the promise less like a demand.
Garrett compared the demands with the retained delivery records only after permission had been given.

The Shinokami collection notice pointed to a Blackhaven market handover. The separate Syndicate order concerned a waterfront shipment. Two threats, two sets of people who could be harmed if he treated one as a distraction from the other.
He wrote them separately.
His parents' deaths remained a question without a proven culprit. The anger he felt at these organisations could not turn the new documents into answers about them.
He stopped with his pen above the page.

It would have been easy to brief the crew as though every enemy belonged to one continuous story about his family. It would have made the work feel personal and urgent. It would also have made the residents props in a story they had never agreed to enter.
He prepared the mission information without exposing witness identities to the crew unnecessarily.
He made copies for the residents before taking the permitted originals back. The people who had supplied them would not have to ask him to see their own records.
When he finished, he could explain what each operation was for without mentioning revenge. He read the explanation once more to make sure that was still true.

GD30.title: Someone who can tell you no

elements.text: “Do you think I'm making promises I can't keep?” Garrett asked.
Rei looked up. “Which promises?”
“The protection work.”
“You haven't told me all of it.”
Garrett described only the public commitment and what he was authorised to share. No witness names, private file contents or Charles information came with the explanation.
Rei listened, then asked, “What happens if someone doesn't want you there?”
“They can refuse.”
“And do your people know that?”
“I told them.”
Rei waited.
Garrett exhaled. “You're asking if they believe I'll mean it when it makes things harder.”
“Yes.”
“I mean it.”
“I believe you. I don't know everyone who will speak for you.”
The distinction irritated Garrett because it could not be answered by being sincere.
“I can't be everywhere.”
“I didn't ask you to be.”
“Then what—” He stopped, hearing himself turn a useful question into an accusation. “Sorry. Keep going.”
Rei rested his hands on the table. “You wanted people to be able to tell you no. Don't make the first time they do it a test of whether they trust you.”
Garrett sat with that.
“You could have started by saying I was doing a good thing.”
“You asked me a different question.”
He laughed reluctantly. “I did.”
Rei's expression softened. “Do you want encouragement now?”
“A little.”
“Then keep listening when it's inconvenient. That's the part you can practise.”
Garrett did not leave with universal approval. He left with a question he could take to the people who would actually do the work beside him.
Garrett finished the briefing and looked around the room.
“Questions?”
The silence lasted long enough for him to realise the invitation had not made questioning him easy.
“I mean questions,” he said. “Not a chance to repeat the plan back to me.”
Mina Cho shifted forward.
“If people won't move when we ask, what do you want us to do?”
“Keep the exit open. Explain what we can see. Don't turn an offer to leave into an order to prove they're on our side.”
“And if keeping the exit open means letting somebody else get away?”
Garrett looked at the marked handover on the plan.
“The objective is the people being threatened. Not a fight we can brag about afterward.”
Anton Bellamy asked, “What if the collectors say we’re taking over?”
“They can say it. We don't make it true by collecting money after them.”
Mina glanced toward the door. “Some of us joined because you made it look like we didn’t have to back down.”
Garrett let the words stand. He remembered being sixteen and needing strength to mean nobody could take anything else.
“I know,” he said. “I'm asking you to decide what we're standing there for.”
He went through the roles again, this time leaving room for someone to point out what he had missed. The questions made the plan less flattering and more usable.

GD32.title: The market belongs to its people

elements.text: The residents were packing when the collectors arrived.

Garrett watched someone hesitate with their hands still on a piece of property they did not want to abandon. He understood the instinct to ask for one more minute. He could not turn understanding into a guarantee that another minute was safe.
He checked the exit before looking back at the collection detail.
A shopkeeper looked from the Dragons to the armed detail.
“Do you need us behind you?”
“No,” Garrett said. “Nobody earns their place here by standing behind me. Leave if you want to.”
The collectors demanded the witnesses. Garrett felt the crew watching him for the change from instruction to action.
“They don't belong to you,” he said.
The collectors raised their weapons. Garrett would have to face the detail before he could secure the market.
The collectors were defeated in this incident. Garrett recorded the demands and returned the seized takings to their documented owners. The money had never belonged to him.

Someone began to thank him while still shaking. He answered the practical question first: where they could go, what had actually been secured, what was still uncertain. He did not declare the whole market safe forever because people needed reassurance now.
Garrett asked before picking up the fallen item.
The trader looked at him, then indicated where it belonged.
“Over there.”
He moved it carefully.
“Not that way round.”
He turned it. “Here?”
“Yes.”
The instruction was so ordinary that he nearly smiled. After all the arguments about authority, somebody was letting him be useful without allowing him to be in charge of everything.
The trader checked the returned property.
“Will they come back?”
“I can't promise they won't.”
The answer changed the expression on their face. Garrett wanted to soften it immediately.
“This collection detail is stopped,” he continued. “The reporting route is still there. You can use it.”
“And will somebody listen if it isn't dramatic enough for all this?”
He looked at the disturbed street.
“They need to,” he said. “You shouldn't have to wait for it to look like today.”
The trader nodded without offering him trust on behalf of everyone.
“There's another thing that needs moving,” they said.
“Show me.”
He stayed long enough to do the task, then asked whether there was anything else before leaving. The incident had ended. The work of living in the street had not.

GD34.title: The cost of wearing our colours

elements.text: The runner's first explanation used the word protection three times.
Garrett let him finish, then asked the trader what had been said at their door.
The account did not become less direct because people wearing the runner's colours were listening.
“He said we could lose protection.”
“I was keeping rivals away,” the runner said.
Garrett heard Charles's old argument inside the sentence: deciding for someone, then expecting fear for their safety to explain the decision afterward.
He set the complaint on the table.
“Did you say it?”
“Yes, but—”
“Then start with yes.”
The runner looked around the room. No one rescued him with a joke.
“You know what they're up against.”
“So do they,” Garrett said. “They live there.”
“I wasn't going to hurt them.”
The trader interrupted. “I didn't know that. You were telling me what would happen if I didn't do what you wanted.”
Garrett watched the runner begin another defence, then stop.
“What do you want from me?” the runner asked.
“An accurate account. Restitution. No unsupervised civilian contact.”
“You're removed from protection work. We'll arrange restitution, and your rank does not exempt you from the review.”
“You may participate in restitution under supervision. No civilian contact until review. This is not permission to go back and ask them to make you feel forgiven.”
Garrett turned to the trader. “Is there something we still haven't heard?”
“I want to know I can leave this room without being followed by the argument.”
“You can,” Garrett said. “You don’t owe him a reassuring answer.”
Afterward the crew accepted the written charter. Garrett did not mistake agreement in the room for proof they would never need to test it again.
The proposed bargain was simple enough to be insulting.
An exclusive Red Dragons route. A useful advantage. All Garrett had to do was stop treating the driver and the disputed load as his concern.
He looked at the driver. The person was watching the negotiation with the concentration of someone whose future had become a subject other people were discussing.
“What happens to them?” Garrett asked.
The escort returned to the surcharge and collateral.
“That wasn't what I asked.”
“They remain until the dispute is settled.”
Garrett felt how easily he could turn this into a speech about his own principles. He kept it shorter.
“They get to go home. That's the whole bargain.”
The armed detail moved to block the exit.
The fight's narration follows resolved actions. Garrett can be afraid for someone without knowing their fate before the outcome is determined.
The driver left freely, and the load was returned to its documented owner. Garrett took no cut and acquired no ownership of the people who had needed help.
The driver checked the returned load before looking at Garrett.
“Do I sign something?”
“The property record, where the return needs documenting.”
“I meant for you.”
Garrett shook his head.
“No membership. No cut.”
The driver kept looking at him, as if waiting for the rest of the arrangement to arrive after the generous part.
“You can go,” Garrett said.
“I know you said that.”
He heard the difference. Saying it again more firmly would not make the person less accustomed to hidden conditions.
Instead he moved out of the route they needed to use.
The driver gathered what was actually theirs. Garrett remained nearby while the documented handover finished, without converting the pause into a claim on their gratitude.
When they left, he felt tired enough to notice how much of the last hour he had spent trying not to sound like someone who could decide everything.

He looked at the route he had been offered. It would have been useful. Refusing it did not make him unable to see that. It made the decision something he would have to keep making when the next bargain sounded reasonable.

GD37.title: An ordinary visit
GD37.chapter: Chapter 9 — A brother, not a weapon

elements.text: Charles moved a notebook to clear space.
“You could have left that,” Garrett said.
“I thought you might want somewhere to sit.”
“I can recognise hospitality. It just surprises me here.”
Charles glanced at him. “Would you prefer an instruction?”
“I'm collecting fewer of those.”
A small smile passed between them. Garrett sat before it became something either needed to explain.
Charles asked about the cooking. Garrett answered at more length than the question required, then caught himself watching for the familiar impatience.
Charles was listening.
“You can tell me if you're busy,” Garrett said.
“I made time.”
The words were ordinary. Garrett looked down at his hands so he would not have to make them carry too much in his face.
After a while he said, “I keep wanting every fight to lead to Mum and Dad.”
Charles closed the notebook fully.
“So do I.”
“Even when I know it doesn't. Someone in front of me does something cruel, and part of me wants that to be the answer to everything.”
Charles nodded once. He did not supply a new suspect or confidential laboratory lead to fill the space.
“Am I distracting myself?” Garrett asked. “With the protection work?”
“From what?”
“From finding out.”
“No,” Charles said. “But I used justice to excuse what I did to you. Don't let me teach you that.”
Garrett sat still.
“You're making it sound as though I can't make my own mistakes.”
“You can.”
“Good. I'd hate to be derivative.”
Charles laughed quietly. Garrett hadn't realised how much he had wanted to hear the sound without a fight on either side of it.
“I want us to talk about this,” Garrett said. “Without every conversation ending in one of us deciding what the other is allowed to survive.”
“I want that too.”
The agreement was not proof they already knew how. It gave them something concrete to attempt the next time fear made certainty seem easier.

GD38.title: Family is not an order
GD38.chapter: Chapter 9 — A brother, not a weapon

elements.text: “If you find something real, tell me what you safely can,” Garrett said. “Don't call me in because you need another pair of hands and tell yourself family makes the answer yes.”
Charles watched him. “The same goes for you.”
“I know.”
“Do you?”
Garrett nearly made a joke, then stopped. “I want to. Remind me if I start doing it.”
“I will.”
“And if all we have is a suspicion?”
“We call it a suspicion.”
Garrett nodded. The agreement left room for information to remain incomplete without either of them disappearing behind it.
“I don't want our contact to depend on having a useful lead,” Garrett said. “Your work stays yours. Mine stays mine. We can still ask whether the other has eaten.”
Charles looked down briefly. “I'd like that.”
“You sound surprised.”
“I didn't realise how much I'd made ordinary things conditional.”
“Then start with something ordinary.”
Charles asked about his day. Garrett gave him an answer that included a small irritation instead of a mission summary.

GD39.title: An anchor, not a throne
GD39.chapter: Chapter 9 — A brother, not a weapon

elements.text: Garrett laid the charter beside the accounts.
One member wanted to charge for the next rescue. Another wanted to follow the defeated crews and make sure they did not return by claiming more ground.
Both suggestions offered a way to make the last victories feel permanent. He understood the attraction before rejecting the proposals.
“If helping becomes a fee they can't refuse, we are collecting,” he said. “If the street becomes ours because we fought there, we are taking it.”
“How do we keep doing this, then?” someone asked.
That was the useful question. It did not accuse him of weakness or ask him to promise an endless supply of personal effort. It asked what would happen after the meeting.
“We make it work without waiting for me to be the person someone finds,” Garrett said. “A standing rota. Clear responsibility. People can request help and refuse it.”
He listened to practical objections about availability and responsibility rather than treating them as disloyalty. The rota would have to be maintained by people who could ask for help themselves.
“Then residents need a continuing way to tell us what they need and what we've done wrong,” Garrett said. “A council that isn't just another room where our rank decides who gets heard.”
“Even when they ask us to stay away?”
“Especially when that's the answer we don't want.”
He recorded the commitment to a resident-led council. Agreeing to hear people was the beginning; he could not declare their consent on their behalf.

Neither rival had been destroyed. Garrett could feel the unfinished scale of the problem without deciding that every useful thing must therefore be too small. The Dragons would be judged by what happened after the meeting.
The note was short.
Still here. Toast the shells first.
Garrett laughed, then put it down because reading it again immediately felt too much like checking whether it would disappear.

Charles had answered an ordinary argument. He had not sent a revelation about their parents, a demand for help or a reason Garrett should stop asking questions. He had kept a small part of the agreement.
The shopkeeper returned a borrowed bowl. Garrett took it and thanked them. There was no envelope of protection money tucked inside it, no new condition disguising itself as gratitude.
After they left, he placed the bowl where it belonged and looked at the note again.
He missed Charles. Finding him had not made that feeling foolish. It had given it somewhere less frightening to go.
He wrote a private reply, then began preparing the meal. It was personal, with no operational details: an answer to a brother who had finally answered him.
He placed the note beside the recipe. He could answer later. Tonight he could eat without arranging company to prove he was coping.

There would be requests and arguments tomorrow. Tonight was not a victory over grief. It was an evening he could inhabit without waiting for a ringing phone to tell him whether his life was allowed to continue.
Rei lifted one of the dumplings from the tray and turned it between his fingers.
Garrett pointed at him with the spoon. “Don't start.”
“I haven't said anything.”
“You've got the expression.”
“What expression?”
“The one where you decide something I've cooked needs a character study.”
Rei looked at the dumpling again. “This one has had a difficult afternoon.”
“It was fine until you picked it up.”
“So was the first one.”
Garrett laughed before he could stop himself. The sound surprised him; he hadn't realised how long he had been standing there without making one.
Rei put the dumpling down gently.
“You still keep it?” he asked.
“Which?”
“The drawing of you stealing one.”
“In the till.” Garrett reached for another wrapper. “Different drawing. Your first complaint was the split seam.”
“It wasn't a complaint.”
“I know that now. You could have made it clearer before I wondered whether you were going to review the whole menu in pictures.”
“You remembered my order.”
“You kept coming back.”
“I didn't always order.”
Garrett looked up. Rei was concentrating on folding a wrapper, giving him room to decide whether to answer that.
“No,” Garrett said. “You didn't.”
For a few moments, the only conversation was the tray moving between them.
Then Garrett said, “I'm glad you did.”
Rei glanced at him. The reply took a moment.
“Me too.”
Garrett pressed the edges of his dumpling together too firmly. A little filling escaped.
Rei looked down at it.
“Don't,” Garrett said.
“I could draw that one.”
“You could put it in the pot.”
Rei laughed and reached for the tray. Garrett let him take it, then asked how his day had been. This time he waited for the whole answer.
“You're doing it again,” April said.
Garrett looked down at the papers, then at the food.
“These are different papers.”
“I had noticed the absence of shipping stamps.”
He put them away. “Dinner first?”
“Dinner with me. You can eat and still be somewhere else.”
He gave her a rueful smile. “That's annoyingly specific.”
“I've collected evidence.”
He laughed and asked her a question he meant to hear the answer to. They could still argue about how well he was doing this without turning every correction into proof he had failed her.
“Did you get the bowl back?” she asked.
“Yes.”
“And put it away?”
“I am capable of completing a task.”
“I know. I'm asking whether this one is complete.”
He smiled. The question did not concern a missing man or a new threat. He answered it, then asked which ordinary job she wanted help with.

GD43.title: Direct encounter route
GD43.chapter: Alternate routes, state variants and verification

elements.text: Garrett recognised Charles before the room made sense around him.
For a moment he stopped moving. He had thought so often about finding him that he expected recognition to feel rehearsed. Instead it took away every prepared word.
“Charles?”
His brother turned.
Garrett looked again, searching for the small differences that would prove this was somebody else and return the world to the question he already knew how to live inside.
There was no mistake.
“You're here.”
Charles glanced toward the door. “Garrett. Lower your voice.”
That made the recognition worse. It was his brother's voice, his brother's instinct to instruct him, alive and close enough to be angry with.
“Don't start there,” Garrett said.

RD01.title: The blank spaces
RD01.chapter: Chapter 1 — Two pages on the table

elements.text: Rei knew the notebook belonged to him before he recognised anything inside it.
There was a pressure to the handwriting, the same habit of bearing down at the end of a line. He still did it when he was tired. He passed a finger beside the letters without touching them.
A timetable. Instructions divided into intervals.

He remembered counting those intervals. That much came without effort. When he tried to follow the memory farther, there was no room around it, no continuous sequence he could walk through. He looked up at his own table and waited until the present settled around him again.
Yuriko had left the book with him years ago. It had not arrived today with a message he had failed to understand. Nothing about the paper had changed because he had finally opened it.
He brought out a drawing made after they had escaped and placed it beside the timetable.
The difference between the pages bothered him. He had expected to be able to recognise himself more easily in one than the other. Instead he recognised the pressure of his hand in both.
“I made this too,” he said.
The words sounded oddly formal in the empty room. He looked at the drawing again.
No one had assigned it to him. He had chosen where the first line went.

He wrote down what he could actually read and what he remembered of counting. When he reached the point where the memory stopped, he stopped writing. The empty space looked deliberate now. He left it there.
He closed the book halfway, stood and felt the floor beneath both feet. The table was his table. The drawing was still beside the notebook when he sat again. He recorded only what was on the page.

The old seal matched the name on a present-day Kurose House notice. A name surviving did not tell him who had survived with it, or whether anyone had. He wanted records he could check without asking his memory to manufacture the missing years.

RD02.title: You can close the book
RD02.chapter: Chapter 1 — Two pages on the table

elements.text: Yuriko stopped when she saw the notebook.
“You found it.”
“I knew where it was.” Rei looked down. “I opened it.”
She nodded, accepting the difference. For a moment he wished she would say something ordinary enough to make him stop waiting for her reaction.
“Do you want me to sit?” she asked.
He moved a chair away from the table with his foot.
“I recognised the writing,” he said. “Then I couldn't tell whether I remembered what it said or just remembered being told things like it.”
Yuriko leaned forward only far enough to see the part he turned toward her.
“I don't want to answer that for you.”
“You were there.”
“Not everywhere you were.”
He looked at her. She was holding herself carefully, as though trying not to take up space he had not offered.
“I know,” he said. “Sorry.”
“You can ask me. I just need to be allowed to say I don't know.”
Rei glanced at the other drawing. “I keep thinking I should be able to look at a page.”
“You are looking at it.”
“Without doing this.”
“Doing what?”
He couldn't find a description that didn't sound smaller than it felt.
Yuriko waited. Then she said, “Would you like me to put the other things away? Or leave them?”
“Leave them.”
“All right.”
He let the notebook close. She did not look relieved, which he was grateful for. It would have made him feel as though he had completed a task for her.
“I don't want to show you yet.”
“Then don't.” She pulled the chair a little farther from the page. “Do you want me here anyway?”
He nodded.
“Can we talk about something else?”
“Yes. But you might have to help me choose it.”
That made him look up. She gave him a small, uncertain smile. He had been so occupied with finding the right response that he had forgotten she might be searching too.

RD03.title: The usual
RD03.chapter: Chapter 1 — Two pages on the table

elements.text: Garrett looked up when Rei came in.
“The usual?”
Rei took longer than he meant to answer.
“Or something else,” Garrett added. “I do know more than one order.”
“The usual is fine.”
“Good. I'd have had to defend my reputation.”

Rei sat where he could watch Garrett work. The familiarity of it loosened something he had been carrying without noticing: a question asked because someone wanted to feed him, an answer that did not need supporting documents.
When Garrett set the plate down, one dumpling had opened along its seam.
“Before you say anything—”
“I wasn't going to.”
“You're looking at it professionally.”
Rei turned the plate a little. “It has character.”
Garrett stopped, then laughed. “Still using that excuse?”
The old phrase brought back the first visit so clearly that for a moment the room seemed to contain both evenings.

RD04.title: The split dumpling
RD04.chapter: Chapter 1 — Two pages on the table

elements.text: FLASHBACK — Golden Dragon, early months
Rei had come in alone after a shoot. He wanted food and a place where no one was asking him to hold a position. His sketchbook rested against his leg beneath the table.
“Give me that one. I’ll replace it.”
“It’s all right.”
“It’s opened.”
“I can see that.”
Rei pulled the receipt closer and drew the crooked seam. When Garrett returned, he glanced at the paper.
“Is that a complaint?”
“It has more character than the intact ones.”
“That sounds suspiciously like a polite complaint.”
“I ate it.”
“A committed critic.”
Rei felt himself smile before he decided whether to encourage him.
“Can I keep that?”
“What for?”
“To remember the standard I’m being held to.”
“It isn’t a standard.”
“Good. I was worried I’d have to break one on every plate.”
Rei pushed the paper toward him. Garrett pinned it up rather than dropping it beside the till. Rei watched the small care with which he straightened it.
“You don’t have to display it.”
“I know.”
For once, Rei had no answer ready. He finished his meal more slowly than he needed to.
PRESENT DAY
Garrett was still standing beside the table, watching Rei's expression.
“You went quiet.”
“I was remembering.”
“The review?”
“The first time.”
Garrett's smile softened. “You can stay a while this time too.”
Rei looked at the food. He had records to ask for, and he would ask for them. He did not have to leave before finishing dinner to prove how much they mattered.
The dates were clear.

Rei checked them again anyway, following the same line with his finger. The original organisation had ended. A later one had taken the name. Records had passed between hands; that did not mean the people he remembered had returned.
He had been afraid of an answer he could recognise immediately. The actual one required him to sit still and read.

The retained training ledger described imposed drills and punishment. His name occupied a space in a record someone else had decided to keep. There was no account of what the room had felt like to him, no indication that anyone had considered the intervals too long for a child.
He took the copy he was permitted to make and put it beside his notes.
“So it happened.”

He regretted saying it. He had not needed the ledger to make his life real. Yet seeing the corroboration affected him, and he did not know how to admit that without sounding as though he had doubted himself completely.
The filing did not restore a voice, a face or a missing hour. He waited for something to arrive. Nothing did.
After a while he wrote: The document confirms this. I do not remember all of it.
Both sentences could stay.

The current records named Kurose House, the riverside annex and the supply house, along with the successor's administrators. Those were places and people he could ask about in the present. He copied their dates carefully, keeping the old organisation and the new one on separate lines.
“I found records,” Rei said.
Yuriko looked at the folder but did not reach for it. “Do you want me to read them?”
“Not all of them.”
He selected the page he was prepared to share. It took longer than handing her the whole folder would have. She waited without watching his hands too closely.
When she finished, she put it down between them.
“I don't remember this happening to you.”
“I didn't think you would.”
“I don't mean—”
“I know.”
But he had answered too quickly. Her face changed, and he realised she had been trying to say more.
“Sorry,” he said. “Go on.”
“I mean I can believe you without having a memory to put beside it.”
He looked at the page. “I keep asking myself why I remember one part so clearly and not the thing next to it.”
“I can't tell you why.” She folded her hands in her lap. “There are things I remember differently from the way you talk about them. I worry you'll think I'm saying yours are wrong.”
“I don't want you to agree with me just to make it easier.”
“Then don't ask yourself to agree with a whole record at once either. Read what it actually says.”
He almost smiled. “You sound like you've been waiting to tell me that.”
“I've been waiting for a chance to finish a sentence.”
He gave a brief, surprised laugh. She looked relieved for herself this time, and he understood it.
“Finish it.”
“I want us to be able to talk without one of us having to remember enough for both.”
Rei moved the folder away from the space between them.
“I want that too.”

“I found something. I’m not ready to show it.”

“Then we can leave it closed,” Yuriko said. “You don’t have to pretend you found nothing.”
Emily had two pieces of paper laid out beside her work.
“Which one?” she asked.
Rei looked at them. “For what?”
“The backing. The first one makes the colour softer. The second makes it stand out.”
“What do you want it to do?”
She gave him a look. “I was hoping you would answer that part.”
He bent closer. For several minutes he had to think about nothing but the edges of the paper and the way one colour changed another. He hadn't noticed how hungry he was for a question of that size.
“The second,” he said. “But turn it.”
“Like this?”
“A little more.”
She moved it too far on purpose.
“Perfect,” he said. “Now no one can see the work at all.”
Emily laughed and set it straight.
After a while she asked, “Do you want to tell me how you've been?”
He kept looking at the paper. “I don't know how to make it a short answer.”
“It doesn't have to be short.”
“I don't know if I want the long one either.”
She nodded. “Then you can hold this corner while I fix it.”
“You don't mind?”
“I asked you here because I wanted your opinion. I still want it.”
He placed his hand where she indicated. She adjusted the backing, frowned, then reached for the first sheet again.
“You're ignoring my opinion.”
“I'm considering it. That's different.”
He smiled. For once, being unable to settle something did not mean either of them was in trouble.

RD08.title: No need to fill the silence

elements.text: “Do you want an answer,” Garrett asked, “or do you want me to listen?”
“I haven't asked anything yet.”
“You've been staring at the same clean bowl for a while.”
Rei set it down. “What if I tell you something and then have to say I don't remember the part you're going to ask about?”
“Then I'll stop asking about that part.”
“You make it sound easy.”
“I didn't say I'd never get it wrong.” Garrett passed him a dry cloth. “You can tell me when I do.”
Rei took it. The small division of work—the wet bowls, the drying, the places they knew without asking—brought back how long it had taken to become ordinary.
FLASHBACK — Later visits, after their first meeting
Garrett remembered his order the next time. Rei told himself that was a good reason to return again. The food was good. It was on his way often enough. He could sit without being hurried.
On a later evening, Garrett asked about the sketchbook and actually waited while Rei explained what he was trying to make.
Another night, Rei stayed while the bowls were washed.
“You don't have to do that,” Garrett said when Rei picked up a cloth.
“I know.”
Garrett looked at him, then slid a bowl within reach.

The silence after that lasted long enough for Rei to wonder whether he was expected to repair it. Before he could think of a subject, Garrett began talking about something that had gone wrong in the kitchen. He didn't ask why Rei was quiet.
Eventually there was an evening when Rei came in after he had already eaten.
Garrett glanced toward the kitchen. “Food?”
“No. I just—”
He nearly supplied an excuse. Garrett pulled out a chair.
“All right. Sit down.”
PRESENT DAY
Rei finished drying the bowl.
“I don't have a whole story to tell you tonight.”
Garrett placed another bowl beside it. “You didn't have one the first time either.”
“I had a complaint.”
“No, apparently you had an artistic assessment.”
Rei shook his head. He stayed. He could share a little, or nothing more, and the chair remained his to use.
Rei opens the kept storyboard alone. Its crooked miniature roof recalls the work of holding it still, before the page recalls any later loss.
FLASHBACK — High-school lunch break
“Hold the pigeon there,” Marcus said. “No, higher. It has a very important bus to miss.”
Rei looked at the timetable. “This says it arrives yesterday.”
“Public transport with ambition.”
“That's not what ambition means.”
“Fine. Public transport with a serious administrative problem. Hold still.”
The roof slipped. Rei caught it before it flattened the cardboard street.
Marcus lowered his hands. “A very local weather event.”
“You built a roof that doesn't fit.”
“You moved the building.”
“Because the pigeon couldn't get past it.”
For a moment neither spoke. Marcus looked between the pieces, annoyed enough that Rei wondered whether he should offer to start again.
Instead Marcus picked up the pencil.
“If I make the street wider, it stops looking like the place I wanted.”
“Then let it get in the way.”
“What?”
“The pigeon can walk around it.” Rei shifted the little bird along the edge of the building. “It misses the bus. It goes past the places the bus doesn't.”
Marcus watched him move it. Then he leaned over the page.
