“Wait. Do that again.”
Rei did.
“Slower.”
“You could say please.”
“Please perform the extremely important pigeon journey again.”
Rei laughed. Marcus was already drawing, tongue briefly caught between his teeth as he concentrated.
“You're changing my whole bit,” Rei said.
“I'm fixing the part where you made it interesting and didn't tell me where it ended.”
“So it was interesting.”
“Don't make me regret saying it.”

They tried the movement again. It took longer than either of them expected. Marcus changed his mind twice and refused to change it a third time. Rei complained, then held the roof where it needed to be.
“You're buying lunch after this.”
“Half my sandwich and a credit bigger than the pigeon.”
“Deal.”
PRESENT DAY

Adult Rei rested his hand beside the drawing. He remembered being hungry and irritated and pleased with their idea. He let all three things remain in the memory. Marcus had been there making decisions, not waiting to become the subject of somebody else's grief.
Emily looked at the storyboard Rei had chosen to bring.
“He could be so stubborn about it.”
Rei glanced up.
She hesitated. “I don't mean that badly.”
“No,” he said. “He could.”
Sophie leaned forward without taking the page. “You were both very certain a cardboard bird needed that much discussion.”
“It did.”
“Apparently.”
Rei found himself defending the idea before he remembered he didn't have to. “It wasn't just the bird. He wanted it to feel like a place.”
Emily nodded. “I liked listening to him explain things. Even when I didn't know how he got from the first thing to the last.”
“He'd get there,” Rei said.
“Eventually,” Sophie said.
He laughed. The laugh stopped abruptly, leaving him embarrassed by how exposed he felt.
Emily looked down at her hands. “I do that too.”
“What?”
“Laugh. Then feel as though I've forgotten something.”
Rei ran his thumb along the edge of the paper. “Sometimes I feel like I'm being dishonest if I talk about a good day.”
Sophie waited before answering. “I don't think a good day stops having happened.”
“I know. It just feels strange.”
“Yes,” Emily said. “It does.”
Neither rushed to make it feel different. Rei looked at the drawing again and told them how Marcus had refused to widen the street. The disagreement mattered to the story. He left it in.

RD11.title: The empty place on the bench

elements.text: The folded corner of the storyboard brought back another school morning. Rei sat at his own table and let the memory come.
FLASHBACK — School courtyard

Rei had kept the next storyboard page flat against his notebook all morning. One corner had folded in his bag anyway. He worked at it with his thumb as he crossed the courtyard, thinking Marcus would notice it before he noticed the drawing.
Emily and Sophie were already at the bench.
There was room between them. Neither moved to fill it.
“Where is he?” Rei asked. “I brought the next page.”
Emily looked at the notebook, then back at him. Her mouth opened, but nothing came out.
“What?” He stopped trying to smooth the corner. “Did I get something wrong?”
“Rei,” she said. “Can you sit down with us?”
He looked at Sophie. She was holding her hands together so tightly that he could see the pressure in her fingers.
“Why? What's happened?”
“We didn't want you hearing it from someone in the corridor,” Sophie said.
“Hearing what?”
Emily drew a breath that caught before she could finish it.
“Marcus died.”
For a moment, Rei waited for the rest. There had to be another part of the sentence, something that changed what those two words meant.
Emily wiped at her cheek with the heel of her hand.
“His family told the school. He died by suicide.”
“No.” Rei heard how flat his voice sounded. He tried again. “No, we were going to finish this.”
He held up the notebook. Neither of them looked away from him.
“The film,” he said, because perhaps they hadn't understood. “I've got the next bit. He said the pigeon could—”
He stopped. He could picture Marcus reaching across the page, impatient to change something. He could almost hear the argument they would have about it.
“He still has my pencil.”
Sophie pressed her lips together. Then she moved her bag off the bench, making room for him.
“I keep looking up,” she said. “Every time someone comes round that corner.”
Rei looked too.
A student he barely knew crossed the courtyard. Someone called to someone else near the doors. Nothing stopped.
He sat because his knees had begun to feel unreliable. The notebook stayed upright in his hands until Emily asked, very quietly, “Do you want me to hold that?”
“No.”
“All right.”
He lowered it onto his lap himself.
“Are they sure?” he asked.
Emily nodded. Tears slipped down her face while she tried to keep looking at him.
“I wish I had something different to tell you.”
“Did he say anything? Did anyone—” Rei swallowed. “Did someone know?”
“I don't know,” she said. “I don't know everything that happened.”
He wanted her to keep talking anyway. Any detail might make this into something with an edge he could hold.
“Joseph knew he was hurting him.”
Sophie's eyes closed for a moment.
“He knew,” Rei repeated. “He watched him. They all did. And then they'd laugh like it wasn't anything.”
“What they did was cruel,” Sophie said. Her voice shook. “I'm not going to pretend it wasn't.”
“Then why didn't anybody stop it?”
Neither answered immediately.

Emily looked down at the notebook. “I keep going over things too. What I saw. What I said. What I should have said.” She caught herself and shook her head. “I don't have an answer that makes this make sense.”
Rei rubbed his thumb against the folded corner again. It had softened until it would no longer lie flat.
“I should have stayed with him.”
“Rei—”
“I could have. There were times I could have stayed.”
Emily shifted closer, leaving a little space between them.
“You were his friend,” she said. “You cared about him. That part is true.”
“It didn't help.”
“You don't know that.” Her voice broke. She waited before trying again. “You don't know that being his friend meant nothing to him.”
Rei stared at the page until the lines blurred. The little buildings were still there. The pigeon was still waiting for a bus that made no sense.
“I don't want this to be the only thing I can remember now.”
Sophie wiped her face with her sleeve.
“Then we can talk about the other things,” she said. “When you want to. Not all now.”
“I don't think I can go into class.”
“We can go to the counsellor,” Emily said. “I'll come with you.”
“Me too,” Sophie said.
“Not yet.”
“All right.”
Rei's breathing caught. He tried to hide it by bending over the notebook, but that only brought the drawings closer.
“Can you just stay here?”
Emily settled beside him. “Yes.”
Sophie stayed on his other side. No one reached for the page again.
He could not think further ahead than that: the bench, the notebook, the two of them staying. For a while, they let that be enough to do.
PRESENT DAY
Rei became aware of the room by degrees: the chair under him, the light across his table, the page he had been holding too tightly.
He put it down before the corner tore.
For a moment he wanted to apologise to it. The thought made him close his eyes. It was paper. He could take care of it, but taking care of it could not change that morning.

He sat until he could look at the drawing without trying to force himself back into the courtyard. Later, if Sophie was available and he chose company, he would meet her somewhere they could walk. He did not need to make that arrangement before he had finished breathing through this moment.
“Do you have somewhere in mind?” Sophie asked.
“No.”
“Good. I was going to pretend I did.”
Rei looked at her. She lifted one shoulder, and he felt the first small release of tension since leaving home.
They walked for a while without discussing why he had asked to meet. He noticed that she slowed when he did without making an announcement of it.
“You can walk normally,” he said.
“I am.”
“You're matching me.”
“That is normal when I'm walking with someone.”
He almost apologised. Instead he said, “I don't know what I want to talk about.”
“Then we can find out.”
“And if I don't?”
“We'll still have walked somewhere.”
A few steps later he said, “I remembered the bench.”
Sophie looked ahead. “Oh.”
He appreciated the smallness of the answer. She didn't ask him to describe everything.
“I thought I was remembering the film. Then I was back there.”
“Do you want to stop?”
“No. Keep walking.”
She did.
After a while she said, “I don't always know whether asking makes it worse.”
“It helps that you ask me.”
“All right.”
“And that you don't look disappointed when I don't know.”
Sophie gave him a brief sideways glance. “I have plenty of other things to be disappointed in. Your directions, for example.”
“We don't have a destination.”
“Exactly. Terrible planning.”
He laughed softly. They kept walking, and he did not have to explain the laugh either.

Alone again, Rei remembered Joseph treating the bullying as something too small to answer for. The storyboard lay on the table in front of him. He let the present settle before following the memory farther.
FLASHBACK — Outside the school administration entrance
“Joseph.”
Joseph turned, impatience already on his face. “What?”
Rei had wanted him to turn. Now that he had, the words Rei had rehearsed no longer came in order.
“You don't get to talk about him like that.”
“Like what?”
“Like none of it mattered.”
Joseph looked toward the building. “I'm not doing this.”
“You took his things. You made everybody look. You waited until people were watching.”
“It was school. People get picked on.”
“His name was Marcus.”
“I know his name.”
“Then say it.”
Joseph tried to move past him. Rei stepped into his way.
“You think shouting at me changes anything?” Joseph said.
Rei wanted a reaction that would make the weeks of cruelty visible. He wanted Joseph to stop looking inconvenienced.
He shoved him against the wall and punched him. Joseph staggered and raised his arms. Rei lunged again before a teacher pulled him back.
“Rei. Step back. Now.”
“Let go.”
Another member of staff moved toward Joseph. Rei struggled once, then stopped when he realised he was still trying to reach him.
“You saw what he did,” he said. He was no longer sure who he was saying it to. “Where were you then?”
“We will take a statement about that. Right now, you attacked another student. You're coming to the office.”
Later, the suspension decision lay between him and the headteacher. His guardian would be contacted. There would be a return meeting. The bullying report would be addressed separately.
“So he gets to go back,” Rei said, “and act like it was nothing.”
“The suspension is for your actions today.”
He looked at his hand. It hurt. He had imagined Joseph's pain would make him understand something. He could not tell whether Joseph understood anything more than he had before.
Outside, Rei folded the letter around the unfinished storyboard. He walked away with both of them.
PRESENT DAY

He laid the remembered sequence beside the present feeling without pretending he was still in it. Being angry had not been the same as knowing what to do. He needed to remember that before deciding what came next.
Garrett put the clean towel down when Rei mentioned Marcus.
“The film?” he asked.
Rei nodded. “I keep coming back to it.”
“You told me about the bus timetable.”
“And the pigeon.”
“And the weather event.” Garrett's expression shifted into a small smile. “You sounded annoyed with him when you told me that part.”
“I was.”
“Good.”
Rei looked at him.
“I mean—” Garrett stopped. “That came out wrong.”
“No. I think I know.”
Garrett leaned back against the counter. “He gets to be somebody who annoyed you too. From the way you talk about him, I don't think he'd have made that difficult.”
Rei laughed, then looked down.
“I worry I'm telling the same story too often.”
“You haven't made me learn it for a test.”
“Garrett.”
“I don't mind hearing it.” The answer came without a joke this time. “I didn't know him. This is how I get to know something about him.”
Rei let that sit between them.
“Joseph still makes it small,” he said eventually.
Garrett's hands tightened briefly around the edge of the counter. “I remember you telling me.”
“I don't need you to do anything.”
“All right.”
The quick agreement surprised him.
“You can be angry,” Rei said.
“I am. I can be angry and stay here.”
Rei looked toward the unfinished cleaning. “You were working.”
“It'll wait.”
For once, Rei believed him without trying to calculate how much of a burden the waiting made him.
Back home, Rei opened to the miniature city again.

There was a temptation to make the page carry a conclusion: something he had learned, something he could finally promise. He could not find a sentence that did not ask too much of a drawing two boys had made during lunch.

He began with the crooked roof. Then the argument about the street. He wrote that Marcus had made him laugh and sometimes made him impatient. When he reached Joseph's bullying, he recorded what he knew without making it the only thing on the page. He did not invent the words Marcus had never had a chance to say to him.

He chose a place he could reach without having to unpack a whole history first. He moved it twice before leaving it there. It did not have to become a display he explained to visitors. He could come back to it privately.

The gaps in his childhood memory and the grief he remembered from school were different things. He did not need to make either explain the other. He closed his notes when he had written what he could honestly say.

RD16.title: The consent that was not there

elements.text: Rei nearly began with Joseph's name.
He stopped himself. The person at the desk had not been in the school courtyard. He had come for a form, and he needed to ask for the form.
“I'm looking for the public participation information.”
Robin provided the published material. Rei read the withdrawal clause once, then again.
“This refers to a separate contract.”
“The procurement reference is there.”
“Can I get a copy of that here?”
“The reference identifies the archive copy.”
He looked back at the page. “This doesn't tell me what happens if someone changes their mind.”
“I can give you the public form. I can't answer for records I don't have.”
The restraint in the answer irritated him before he recognised that it was reasonable. He had no basis to decide what Robin knew about the programme beyond the material being supplied.
“Right,” he said. “Thank you.”
He nearly added another question that was really an accusation. Instead he compared the project number and noted the source.

Outside, he stood with the form held flat between his hands. The referral and the contract shared a reference. That warranted another question. It did not turn the person at the desk into an accomplice or put him any closer to knowing what Joseph would admit.
The complaint was anonymised. Rei read it without trying to supply a face.
People had attempted to withdraw. The records described restraint trials. The authorisation bore Joseph's name.
He went back to the dates, the project number, the connection to the contract. He needed the connection to hold without his anger holding it together.
It did.

For a while he could hear nothing in the room except paper moving beneath his hands. He thought of the participation form, its careful headings, the space where a person could have believed they were being asked.
“They said they wanted to stop,” he said quietly.
This time the sentence belonged to the documents in front of him. He did not need a school memory to make the conduct wrong.

He kept the authorisation with the complaint and left the unanswered questions visible. The equipment records identified the compound and offices. He copied what he would need before approaching headquarters.
He wanted to ask Joseph whether he remembered every person he had made feel small. But that was not the question that would stop the programme.
Rei closed the folder with both hands.
First, what was happening now. He could carry the rest without pretending it was the only reason to act.

RD18.title: A first draft, not a rescue

elements.text: “Can you read this?” Yuriko asked.
Rei reached for the pages. “Of course.”
“Actually read it.”
He looked up.
“Not the way you read something when you've already decided to tell me it's good.”
“I don't do that.”
“You get very quick at the end.”
He looked down at the draft, caught. “All right. I'll be slower.”
“That isn't exactly what I'm asking.”
He smiled and began again.
For a while she found small things to do elsewhere in the room. He could tell she was listening for the page turns. When he finished, she returned too casually.
“Well?”
“I understood what you were trying to do here.” He indicated a passage. “Then I wasn't sure why it changed.”
She frowned. “That was the part I liked.”
“You asked.”
“I know. I'm being gracious.”
“Very.”
She sat beside him and explained. He listened, then read the passage again.
“That isn't all on the page yet,” he said.
Yuriko looked annoyed for a moment, then thoughtful. “Will you read it when I change it?”
“Yes.”
“You don't have to promise immediately.”
“I want to.”
She gathered the pages, leaving the difficult one on top.
“Thank you.”
Rei had come into the room expecting to be asked how he was managing. It was a relief to have helped with something that belonged to her, and to know that helping had included disagreeing.

RD19.title: The successor answers
RD19.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: Rei heard the name of the organisation before he sat down.

The familiarity of it did not make the room familiar. He made himself look at what was actually there: three people waiting for his questions, records placed where he could read them, a chair he had not been ordered to occupy.
Emi spoke first.
“The name frightens you for a reason.”
He stayed standing a moment longer. “You don't know all the reasons.”
“No,” she said. “I don't.”
The admission was preferable to sympathy that claimed too much.
Ren moved the records toward him. “The current roster. The departure records. You can compare them with the filings.”
“Everyone here chose to come?”
“Adults only,” Emi said. “No child recruitment. No training through torture. Adults can leave.”
Rei sat and began reading. He did not want the conversation to make the documents unnecessary. They let him take the time.
When he looked up, Daichi was waiting.
“You kept the name,” Rei said.
“Yes.”
“Then you don't get to ask me to hear something different when you say it.”
“I haven't asked you to.”
“Not yet.”
Daichi accepted the correction without smiling. “What happened to you was wrong. I cannot make this place an answer to it.”
Rei looked back at the records. They matched the current filings. The evidence did not become less persuasive because he disliked what it required him to distinguish.
“And you would let me lead it?”
“I would relinquish command,” Daichi said. “Under that charter. You would be responsible for what happens here now.”
“That's a lot to put in front of someone with this history.”
“Yes.”
“Do you want me to make you feel forgiven?”
“No. I cannot ask you to call this home.”
Rei rested his hands on either side of the papers. He had expected to spend the meeting trying to make someone acknowledge the past. Now the past had been acknowledged, and the decision still hurt.

RD20.title: Outside Kurose House
RD20.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: Outside, Rei stopped before choosing a direction.
He could still hear the name in Daichi's voice. A present-day voice. He had spent much of the meeting making sure he did not confuse that with another one.
The records mattered. He had asked for evidence and received it. He could not decide that evidence only counted when it made the choice easier.
But the documents did not have to live with the sound of the name afterward. He did.

If he led, he would be responsible for people whose lives were not an extension of his past. If he left, he would have to let the organisation continue without making its future his task. If he dismantled it, he would be acting against the successor that existed now, not reaching backward to the original clan.
He stood until those were three separate thoughts.
“I don't have to answer in that room,” he said.
No one had followed him out to insist otherwise.

He could seek company, ask a question or take time alone. Whatever he chose next, he wanted to be able to name what he was choosing, rather than discovering later that he had asked one decision to settle everything.

RD21.title: The decision is still yours
RD21.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: “What would you want me to do?” Rei asked.
Emily looked at him for a long moment. “Do you want my answer, or a reason you won't have to be angry with yourself?”
He looked away. “That's a horrible question.”
“I know. I'm sorry.” She shifted her hands in her lap. “I don't mean you're trying to put it on me.”
“I might be. A little.”
She nodded. “I wish I could make it easier.”
“You don't have to say the right thing.”
“Good, because I don't know what it is.”
The honesty made him smile briefly.
Emily continued, “If you take responsibility, I want you to have room to be a person outside it. If you walk away, I don't want you to think that means you didn't face anything.”
“And if I make a choice you don't like?”
“I might tell you I don't like it.”
He looked at her again.
“I would still want to understand why,” she said.
Rei exhaled. He had not known how much he had been waiting for a promise of approval until she offered something less comfortable and more believable.
“You've asked me three different questions,” Sophie said. “Which one do you want to answer first?”
“I thought I asked what you think.”
“You asked whether you could do it, whether you should, and whether you'd regret it.”
“I'd like one answer that covers all three.”
“So would I. Very convenient.”
He rubbed a hand over his face, almost laughing.
Sophie leaned forward. “I think you should be allowed to want a life that isn't built around answering them.”
“That doesn't tell me what to choose.”
“No.” She paused. “I can stay while you work it out. I can't promise to make it painless.”
“What if I keep changing my mind?”
“Then tell me what changed. We can talk about that instead of starting the whole argument again.”

“I can’t explain the details,” Rei said.

His friend accepted the boundary. They could sit together without opening the file. He did not have to turn privacy into an excuse to leave.

RD22.title: I will listen; I will still ask
RD22.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: Garrett listened until Rei had finished the part he was willing to tell.
Then he said, “What do you want to be different when it's done?”
Rei looked at him. “I want it to be done.”
“I heard that.”
“Then why ask?”
“Because I don't know what done means here.”
Rei stared at the table. The question felt unfair because he had asked himself a version of it already and had not found an answer he liked.
“You think I'm doing this for the wrong reason.”
“I think you have more than one reason.” Garrett paused. “I do know what that feels like.”
Rei looked up again. Garrett did not explain the comparison. He simply stayed with the question.
“If I leave it alone, it still exists.”
“Yes.”
“If I take it on, it becomes something I have to keep answering for.”
“Yes.”
“You could be more helpful.”
“I could agree quickly. You'd notice.”
That earned a tired laugh.
Garrett lowered his voice. “I don't want to tell you something big enough to stop you hearing yourself. I can ask the irritating question and stay for the answer.”
“And if I don't have it tonight?”
“Then you eat before you try again.”

Rei looked at the food between them. He had begun the evening wanting someone to make his uncertainty feel unreasonable. Garrett was refusing to do that, which was annoying in exactly the way a best friend could afford to be.

RD23.title: Accepting responsibility
RD23.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: “I'll do it,” Rei said.
Daichi waited rather than answering too quickly.
“Under the charter,” Rei added. “The parts about leaving. The parts about who doesn't get recruited. They don't become things we say because I'm in the room.”
“They remain the rules,” Daichi said.
“I want the records kept. I want to be able to see when something isn't working.”
Ren glanced at the existing papers. “We can begin with what is already documented.”
Rei nodded. Begin. He had been thinking about a decision as though its hardest part would be saying it.
Daichi relinquished command under the established conditions. Emi and Ren remained colleagues, not people whose private trust had been magically awarded to him.
When the meeting ended, Rei found himself with a question about an ordinary administrative detail. He asked it. Ren answered without treating it as a test of his right to be there.
Later, alone, he put the current papers away separately from the childhood notebook.

He had chosen work that would need doing tomorrow. That was what the decision had given him: responsibility, not ownership of the past. He was allowed to feel the weight of it without pretending certainty had arrived with the title.

RD24.title: Leaving without pretending
RD24.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: “I've read what you gave me,” Rei said. “I believe what these records establish about the current organisation.”
Daichi nodded.
“That doesn't make me want a place in it.”
“It doesn't have to.”
Rei had expected resistance. Without it, he almost continued arguing anyway.
“I don't want to be asked again because someone decides I need more time.”
“Understood.”
“And I am not telling you how to feel about that.”
Daichi's expression stayed measured. “You have given us an answer.”
Rei looked once more at the room. It would continue to exist when he left. There were people here who would have tomorrow's concerns without him being responsible for all of them.
Outside, he waited for the relief he thought should follow a boundary clearly stated. At first there was only tiredness.
Then he realised he could decide where to go next without returning to finish the conversation.
It was a small freedom, too ordinary to announce. He stood with it for a while before walking on.

RD25.title: Choosing to dismantle
RD25.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: “I understand the distinction you're asking me to make,” Rei said. “I am not saying the original clan is still here.”
Daichi's face became more guarded.
“But I've decided to dismantle this organisation.”
There was a pause. Ren drew the current records closer.
“Then we disagree about what should happen to it,” Daichi said.
“Yes.”
Rei heard how little the word explained. There was no sentence he could add that would make the people in the room experience his choice exactly as he did.
He left with the decision made and the required actions still ahead. The organisation remained operational. He could not narrate an ending into existence because he had said what he intended.
The operations had closed. The staff survived and left their organisational duties. Rei recorded the outcome in plain language, then read it again.
He had wanted to know what would remain in him after the name no longer belonged to a functioning organisation he could approach. The answer did not arrive with the final victory.
He could still remember the timetable. The gaps were still gaps.

He sat until he could separate exhaustion from whatever else he was feeling. There would be time to describe it more accurately. For now he would not call the closure a restored childhood, or ask the people who had left to agree that it was.

RD26.title: One thread resolved
RD26.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: Rei returned to the separately kept programme records. Whatever he had chosen at Kurose House, these documents still described people prevented from withdrawing. He did not need to reopen his first decision to recognise the second task. He read the next location and checked what he actually needed before going.

The successor outcome was the last outstanding thread. Rei did not have to invent another immediate task because stopping felt unfamiliar. Home could be a place to pause, not the next problem to solve.

RD27.title: Before you go
RD27.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: “Do you want us to ask you not to go?” Emily said.
Rei looked at her. “I don't know.”
“I don't know whether it would help either.” She rubbed her hands together. “I don't want to say something brave just because you're about to leave.”
Sophie leaned forward. “What can you actually tell us?”
“That I'm going alone. That I don't know how long it'll take.”
“Then don't give us a time you made up,” Sophie said.
He nodded.
Emily looked down, then back at him. “I'd like to see you afterward. That's what I want to say.”
“I'd like that too.”
“Not for a report.”
“I know.”
“And you don't have to be good company.”
Sophie glanced at her. “We were going to tell him that gently.”
Rei laughed despite himself. Emily smiled, then the smile faded into worry she did not try to hide.
“Please be careful,” she said.
He resisted the easy answer that would promise more than he could know.
“I'll pay attention.”
Sophie nodded. “Tell us when you're able. If we agree to wait somewhere, let's actually agree where. No guessing.”
They agreed he would let them know when he was able. Neither friend followed him into the operation. Their worry did not become a promise that everything would be all right.

RD28.title: A place to come back to
RD28.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: Garrett had listened without interrupting. That alone told Rei how much effort he was making.
“You're going to ask,” Rei said.
“Whether you want help?”
“Whether I'm sure.”
Garrett looked at the counter. “Would you believe me if I said I wasn't thinking it?”
“No.”
“Then I won't waste the line.”
Rei smiled faintly.
“I have to go alone.”
“All right.”
“You said that very quickly.”
“I can listen quickly. I'm talented.”
The joke gave them somewhere to stand for a moment.
Then Garrett said, “I don't like not knowing what happens after you leave.”
“I don't know either.”
“I know.” He took a breath. “That's the part I'm having trouble with.”
Rei looked at him. “I don't need you to make it easier to leave.”
“What do you need?”
He considered it.
“Don't make me explain everything when I come back.”
Garrett nodded. “Food first. Details if you want.”
“And if I don't?”
“Then we can have a very serious argument about dumplings.”
Rei felt his shoulders loosen.
“Save me something.”
“I can arrange that.”
The practical answer was easier to carry than a promise of safety. He left the conversation knowing there was somewhere he could arrive without having to begin with a successful ending.

RD29.title: The approach
RD29.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: Rei checked the evidence copy he had retained, then put it away. Carrying proof did not make him immune to what was ahead. He checked the approach before him. This was a mission he would undertake alone.

RD30.title: Before the executive door
RD30.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: For a moment, Rei could hear the school courtyard more clearly than the room he had entered.
He let the memory pass far enough to see what was actually in front of him: Joseph, the executive door, the documents he had brought about a programme operating now.
“I have your authorisation,” Rei said. “They asked to withdraw. You kept them.”
Joseph looked at the papers.
“You brought paperwork into my headquarters and expected me to surrender?”
“I brought proof.”
“You've decided what it means.”
“The records describe restraint trials. Your authorisation keeps people here for weapons-response testing. Tell me which part I'm inventing.”
Joseph's sleeves parted around the reinforced arms. Rei heard the mechanism before the powered frame locked into place.
“Awakened people have advantages the rest of us never chose,” Joseph said. “I built mine.”
“And everyone in those records was supposed to pay for it?”
Joseph's expression hardened. “This is bigger than your old grievances.”
There it was: the invitation to become a boy in a courtyard again, furious enough to lose the sentence he had come to say.
Rei held the papers still.
“You don't get to make what you're doing now disappear by calling me angry.”
“You are angry.”
“Yes.”
The admission seemed to leave Joseph with less to interrupt.
“You hurt Marcus,” Rei said. “You made him afraid of rooms he had to walk into. And then you talked about it as if it was something too small to answer for.”
“That was school.”

“He had a life at school. He made things. He could spend half a lunch break arguing about one piece of cardboard because he wanted it right.” Rei swallowed, then continued. “You don't get to make him small because you've finished thinking about him.”
Joseph shifted. The targeting lights followed Rei's movement.
“You think an apology changes any of it?”
“No. I don't.”
“Then what do you want?”
Rei looked at the authorisation again. The present was still there, even with the memory beside it.
“I'm stopping what you're doing here.”
Joseph brought the weapons online.
“Try.”

RD31.title: What an apology cannot return
RD31.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: The powered frame failed. The fight was over. Rei listened to the machinery falling silent.
Joseph spoke before Rei had decided what he wanted to say.
“I bullied Marcus. I chose to hurt him, and then pretended it didn't matter.”
Rei stood still.
“I am sorry,” Joseph said. “I am sorry for what I did to these people too.”
For years, Rei had imagined making him acknowledge it. He had never imagined the silence immediately afterward with any accuracy.
Marcus did not come into the room. The film remained unfinished. There were still people in this programme who needed the outcome to mean more than a conversation between two former classmates.
Rei secured the research records and disabled the containment controls. The surviving participants could leave.
Afterward, Rei noticed that he was still waiting to feel one clear thing. Relief and anger did not arrive in a useful order. He stopped trying to organise them before leaving.

“Not finished,” Rei said, looking at the unresolved objective when he was able. That was all he could accurately call it. He needed recovery and another assessment, not a story in which the confrontation had supplied closure.

RD32.title: You came back
RD32.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: Sophie saw him before he worked out how to begin.
“Sit down,” she said, then stopped. “If you want. Sorry.”
“I want to.”
She moved a chair clear. He sat without making the movement look easier than it was.
“Do you need something now?”
“Water.”
She brought it and waited while he drank.
“The programme is stopped,” he said. Sophie nodded once. “All right.” She did not ask him to make that mean everything was finished.
“It isn't done,” he said. Sophie sat opposite him. “Then we don't have to pretend it is.”
He looked at the glass.
“I don't know what to say about it.”
“You already asked for water. That was useful.”
He gave a tired breath that almost became a laugh.
“I thought I'd be better at coming back.”
“There's no performance requirement.”
He looked up. Her face was serious despite the wording.
“Can we just sit?”
“Yes.”
For a while she stayed with him without checking whether the silence had improved him. Later she asked about food. He could answer that question too.

RD33.title: The pages he keeps
RD33.chapter: Final chapter — A place in the present

elements.text: Rei put the old timetable and the current records on different parts of the table.
The distinction had become easier to describe. It had not become effortless to feel.

Tomorrow there would be questions from people whose present lives he had agreed to help govern. He would answer them as honestly as he could. The title did not entitle him to call uncertainty weakness in someone else.

The organisation would continue without his oversight. He did not need to invent a daily obligation to check whether leaving had been the correct decision. He had read, asked and chosen. That history belonged in the record too.

The successor's operations were closed. The original childhood still could not be revised. He could record the closure without demanding it produce one particular feeling every time he thought about it.

The Blackstone programme was stopped. Joseph had acknowledged what he had done. Rei kept the acknowledgement in its actual place: something that had happened, not a replacement for what had happened before it.
He opened the storyboard once more. The pigeon was still on the page.
“I'm keeping this,” he said.
There was no one there who needed convincing. He could put it away and return to it another day. He could draw something else without asking whether that meant he had forgotten.
For now, he cleared enough room on the table to begin.

RD34.title: The next ordinary evening
RD34.chapter: Final chapter — A place in the present

elements.text: Garrett gave Rei a job small enough that he suspected it had been selected carefully.
“You can tell me if you just want company,” Rei said.
“I also want those folded.”
“You've given me three.”
“High standards. Start small.”
Rei sat down with the wrappers. Garrett worked beside him, occasionally glancing over without correcting him.
“Are you going to say anything?” Rei asked.
“About the folding?”
“About anything.”
Garrett put down what he was holding.
“I was trying not to ask for a report.”
“You can ask how I am.”
“All right. How are you?”
Rei looked at the little row he had made.
“I don't know yet.”
Garrett nodded. “That's an answer.”
“Not a very helpful one.”
“It tells me not to decide for you.”
Rei sat with that for a moment. Then he asked, “How was your day?”

Garrett began to answer lightly, stopped, and told him about an ordinary irritation instead. Nothing in the account needed to become a clue. Rei listened, disagreed with one small detail, and found himself defending the disagreement with more energy than he expected.
Garrett grinned. “There you are.”
Rei looked down. “I was here before.”
The grin softened.
“Yeah,” Garrett said. “You were. Sorry.”
Rei nudged the tray toward him. “These are better than your first one.”
“Historically inaccurate.”
“You kept the evidence.”
Garrett laughed. Rei let himself enjoy having the last word for as long as it lasted.

RD35.title: A place in the present
RD35.chapter: Final chapter — A place in the present

elements.text: Yuriko put her revised pages down beside Emily's materials.
“No one is allowed to call this a productive afternoon,” Sophie said.
“Why?” Emily asked.
“Because then someone will give me a task.”
Rei passed her the nearest light object that needed moving. “Too late.”
Sophie looked at it, then at him. “I trusted you.”
“You arrived.”
“A terrible mistake.”

Yuriko laughed and shifted the papers out of the way before anyone spilled something on them. Emily asked about the revision. For a while the conversation belonged to the two of them, and Rei found himself listening without waiting for his turn to explain how he was doing.
When Yuriko asked him about the changed passage, he read it again.
“That makes more sense.”
“Do you like it?”
“Yes.”
“You can say both things at once, you know.”
“I'm trying not to be too quick at the end.”
She smiled at the callback. Emily looked between them but didn't ask for an explanation.
Later, Sophie began proposing something for another day. Emily objected to the timing. Yuriko wanted to finish her draft first. Rei listened to them negotiate a plan that did not yet exist.
“What about you?” Sophie asked.
He realised he had been thinking about being invited rather than about whether he could come.
“Ask me again when you've agreed what it is.”
“Very demanding.”
“I've learned from all of you.”
They argued a little longer. Nothing in the room required him to turn the afternoon into proof that he was healed.
When he reached for a fresh page, he was thinking about what he wanted to put on it.

FD01.title: Before opening
FD01.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: Fox noticed the shopkeeper checking the street before turning the sign. He knew the difference between looking for customers and waiting for somebody one did not want to see. It was a useful observation, not yet an explanation. He kept the thought to himself until the person chose to speak.

Gordon had questions prepared. He put them aside long enough to ask whether this was still a good time. A person agreeing yesterday did not become obliged to be ready today, particularly with two investigators standing in the doorway.
“Do you want to do this here?” Gordon asked.
The shopkeeper looked toward the counter. “I need to open.”
“We can keep out of the way,” Fox said.
“You say that. People notice you.”
Fox glanced toward Gordon. “Mostly him.”
The shopkeeper almost smiled, then did not.
Gordon moved away from the centre of the entrance. “We can arrange another time. You decide whether to give an account.”
“I want it stopped. I don't want everyone deciding I've started something.”
“Tell us what actually happened,” Gordon said. “We won't ask you to answer for the whole street.”
The shopkeeper took out the three demands, but kept a hand on them.
“And tomorrow?”
Neither man answered immediately.
“Tomorrow still matters,” Fox said.
“That isn't a promise.”
“No.” He looked at the papers. “It's why we're asking about the contact route as well as the collector.”

The shopkeeper let go of the documents one at a time. The dates were supplied willingly. Gordon checked how each copy had been retained, and Fox listened without turning every uncertain phrase into a reason to interrupt.

FD02.title: The same doorway
FD02.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: At the back of the shop, Gordon stopped short of the threshold.
“Street side?” he asked Fox.
Fox looked past him. “If you're staying with the account.”
“Yes.”
It was a small exchange, complete in a few words. The doorway recalled a time when neither had understood what the other was trying to protect.

FM01.title: The same doorway, years not specified
FM01.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: FLASHBACK — A separate earlier Blackhaven witness-protection incident

Fox had followed a physical lead into the lane. Finding an officer between him and the next turn felt like arriving just in time to be told he was too late. He noticed the uniform before he noticed the worker waiting behind it, and later would remember that order with irritation.

Gordon had a person waiting to leave and an unfamiliar armed man approaching. He could not afford to treat confidence as authorisation. He also could not afford to ignore the way the man had stopped speaking to listen toward the bend.
“Hold there,” Gordon said.
“I need that lane.”
“Then tell me why.”
Fox looked beyond the doorway. “Somebody stopped around the turn.”
“Somebody?”
“Footsteps. Then nothing. Close enough that I would check before taking anyone out.”

Gordon changed his angle and checked. He did not announce that the sound proved an offence. The worker behind him moved forward, then stopped when another person visibly tried to obstruct the departure.
Fox stepped toward the lane.
“Not past me,” Gordon said.
“I'm looking at the obstruction.”
“And I have somebody trying to get out.”
Fox looked behind him properly for the first time.

A brief silence. Then he moved to the street-facing position rather than farther into the lane. Gordon escorted the worker clear while Fox held the street-facing position. The worker cleared the lane; that was the part Fox could see.
When the immediate danger had passed, Fox turned back.
“You could have said you were moving someone.”
“You could have asked before choosing the direction.”
“Would you have told me?”
“Enough to keep you out of the doorway.”
Fox gave a short breath that was not quite a laugh.
“You did check.”
“You gave me something worth checking.”
“That sounded painful to admit.”
“It was less painful than ignoring it.”
Neither offered friendship. They had an account to compare and a person whose safety did not become less important because they had begun arguing.
PRESENT DAY
He took the agreed position. Gordon no longer had to explain the doorway to him, but Fox still wanted the question asked rather than the answer assumed.
PRESENT DAY

The brief acknowledgment from Fox let Gordon return to the shopkeeper without looking over his shoulder to guess where his partner had gone. It was cooperation built out of something they had once done badly.

FD03.title: Terms of help
FD03.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: The shopkeeper pointed to a date.
“That was the second demand. I paid the first because I thought perhaps it would end.”
Fox looked up. “Did they say it would?”
“Not in those words.”
Gordon waited while the shopkeeper considered the distinction.
“I wanted it to mean that,” they said.
Fox nodded once. “All right.”

There were copies of three demands and an account of repeated pressure. No confession from an entire organisation. Gordon stated the difference in the record without making the person repeat the frightening part for emphasis.
Outside the conversation, Fox spoke more quietly.
“We know the point they use. Waiting has a cost.”
“So does acting on an incomplete route,” Gordon said.
“I didn't say wander in.”
“No. Tell me what you want to check first.”
Fox indicated the physical comparison he wanted to make. Gordon described the documentation and protected contact arrangement still needed.
It helped that Gordon asked for the next action instead of asking him to become a more patient person. Fox could explain an action. He could not promise never to resent the waiting.
Fox's urgency was not an obstacle to be removed from the plan. It identified the point at which the plan might become an excuse for delay. Gordon still needed the route corroborated, and said so.

They divided the immediate work explicitly. The shopkeeper was told what they could expect next and what remained uncertain. No one promised that handing over papers would make tomorrow safe by itself.

FD04.title: The wrong familiarity
FD04.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: The chemical note was there. Fox recognised it before he finished crossing the accessible frontage. The difficulty began when recognition tried to turn itself into a conclusion.

Gordon trusted Fox's report of the trace. He did not yet know how many perfectly ordinary places the same report could describe. Asking that question felt more delicate than it should between two people who claimed to value accuracy.
“The envelope and that entrance,” Fox said.
“You're confident?”
“In the trace.”
Gordon looked along the frontage. “How many other doors could it put us at?”
Fox's expression tightened. “You think I imagined it.”
“No. I think we need to know how specific it is.”

A consenting worker identified a routinely used cleaner. With permission, they compared the labelled product, the supply record and other accessible surfaces. The same broad note appeared in more than one ordinary place.
Fox stood beside the original entrance again.
“Common product,” he said.
“Yes.”
“Not a unique source.”
Gordon wrote that down without adding a correction in a different voice.
Fox looked at him. “You can leave the observation in.”
“I was going to.”
The more specific fibres and the observed collection route still mattered. They checked those instead of discarding everything because the first inference had been too large.
Naming the limit himself felt better than defending a claim he no longer believed. It did not make the lost certainty pleasant.
He made sure the record credited the useful observation. An accurate correction did not require making his partner smaller.

FD05.title: The person at the counter
FD05.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: Before the collection encounter, the shopkeeper looked toward the exit they had discussed.
“If I need to stop talking?”
“Stop,” Gordon said. “Tell us what you need.”
Fox checked the actual approach. “You don't have to keep somebody interested for our benefit.”
The collector had not agreed to stop. The opposition on this route would have to be faced before the witness could be safe from this demand.

He had wanted the next step to come quickly. Now it was here, with somebody else standing close enough to live with its consequences. He kept that person in his actual assessment of the scene rather than treating the target as all that mattered.
A plan looked cleaner when nobody had begun to move. Gordon checked the partner beside him. Writing the preparation had not finished his part in it.
At the headquarters review, the shopkeeper’s last question remained with them. “Can I close?” The answer they had given belonged in the account too.
Gordon checked what they had secured before answering. The seized receipt supplied a rail-yard lead. It did not give him a reason to keep a tired witness talking indefinitely.
Fox moved out of the person's way.
“We'll tell you what comes next,” Gordon said. “Through the route we agreed.”
“And if nothing comes next?”
“Then you still hear from us about this report.”
The promise would require follow-through. Gordon wrote the agreed route beside the report, where he would have to see it again.

FD06.title: Names after the report
FD06.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: The report linked the collection cell to the Lantern Crew. Gordon left the wording narrow.
Fox read the relevant line. “Not every member.”
“Not from this evidence.”
“Good.”
Gordon looked up briefly, then continued.
They reviewed the protected contact route and the actual receipt. The next lead was real, but neither had to leave the room before the first case had been described accurately.
Watching Gordon make room for his observations in the account brought back the first time he had expected the uniform to mean his contribution would be edited out.
Fox's attention to the wording reminded him of the first debrief, when every distinction had sounded like a personal slight. It had taken more than a clever answer to change that.

FM02.title: An introduction after the noise
FM02.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: FLASHBACK — Later on the day of their first meeting, then a separately marked later appointment
“Jeremy Gordon,” the officer said.
“Fox.”
“Your account of the lane?”
Fox gave it, briefly. Gordon made notes.
“That's not what I said,” Fox interrupted.
Gordon turned the page so he could read it. “Which part?”
“You've separated the sound from the person.”
“You heard movement before we saw the obstruction.”
“And then there was an obstruction.”
“Yes. Those are two observations supporting the account. I haven't removed either.”
Fox read again.
Gordon added that Fox had changed position to protect the departure. He did not describe the worker's destination.
“So you can put the useful part in,” Fox said.
“That was the intention.”
“You missed the blind bend in your route check.”
Gordon looked at the line he had written about the approach. He amended it.
Fox waited for the amendment to become an argument about his manners. It did not.

The small correction unsettled him more than a defensive speech would have. He knew how to distrust somebody who never admitted being wrong. He had less practice with somebody who could admit it without making a show of virtue.
He did not enjoy having the omission pointed out. Enjoyment was not the criterion. Fox had seen something useful, and an accurate account was worth the discomfort of retaining it.
“Delivery traffic changes this lane,” Fox said. “At another hour, your clear approach isn't clear.”
“Can you show me?”
Fox looked at him. “You?”
“Yes.”
They agreed on a later time. No clearance, private file access or formal appointment as an associate was granted by the exchange.
Gordon arrived himself. Fox was already there.
“You came,” Fox said.
“We agreed.”
“I expected someone carrying your questions.”
“I can carry them.”

Fox led him through the accessible route. Gordon asked about a physical detail, listened to the answer and checked what it would mean at the actual departure time. Fox did not have to exaggerate the usefulness of the detail to keep his attention.
At the doorway, Gordon stepped aside before Fox asked.
“Learning,” Fox said.
“From a demanding instructor.”
It was the first remark Fox did not feel obliged to challenge.
PRESENT DAY
Fox set the current rail receipt beside the completed report. “I'll come for the next check.” Gordon nodded. Neither named the offer loyalty. Both knew it had not been automatic at the beginning.

FD07.title: Two ledgers
FD07.chapter: Chapter 3 — The number on the crate

elements.text: The number matched. Gordon put the receipt beside the ledger entry, aligning the fields.
“There,” he said.
Fox looked from the paper to the visible recorded seal comparison. “Right number. Wrong seal.”
Gordon paused. “Different handling?”
“Possibly. Or the wrong shipment.”

They read the full dated page rather than the isolated number. The numbering cycle mattered. A worker's volunteered explanation could be checked against the original headings; it was not accepted as a convenient excuse without comparison.

He had felt a small satisfaction when the number matched, the relief of a question finally presenting its own answer. Now he needed to put that satisfaction down without treating Fox as the person who had taken it away.
He expected to have to argue harder. Part of him was already preparing a harsher sentence. Gordon's pause gave him time to say the useful version instead.
“The same number in another period,” Fox said.
Gordon compared the dates. “Then this entry doesn't establish our handover.”
“You can say it was the wrong one.”
“It was the wrong one.”
Fox glanced up.
Gordon turned the page. “Now let's find the right one without compensating by rushing.”

They checked date, seal and provenance until the actual handover was corroborated. The other shipment remained outside this enquiry. No crew was intercepted merely because a reused number looked persuasive on paper.

FD08.title: A witness to the working day
FD08.chapter: Chapter 3 — The number on the crate

elements.text: The depot worker looked at the documents without reaching for them.
“I can tell you how the numbering works. I can't tell you who's behind everything that comes through.”
“Start with what you do know,” Gordon said.
Fox asked about the visible frontage seal. The worker described an ordinary part of the process and corrected one term Fox had used.
“All right,” Fox said. “That part.”
The worker relaxed slightly. “People usually want the answer they've brought with them.”
“So do we,” Gordon said. “We're trying to check it first.”
Afterward, Fox stood aside while Gordon compared the statement with the existing record.
“We have the number and the seal now,” Fox said.
“Yes.”
“Then don't make the paper wait for another paper to approve it.”
Gordon looked at him. “I'm recording which original supports which observation.”
“Before somebody tells you I imagined the seal?”
“Before either of us forgets what we actually checked.”
Fox considered that, then gave the exact comparison again without the sarcasm.
There were easier ways to share a working day than having every pause examined. Fox also noticed when a pause had no useful purpose. Gordon kept the necessary one and abandoned the rest.
Gordon's work could look like delay from the wrong angle. Standing close enough to see what he was writing made it harder to dismiss the difference.
The supported consignment, not the rejected shipment, remained the courier objective.

FD09.title: What survives the handover
FD09.chapter: Chapter 3 — The number on the crate

elements.text: Gordon placed the recovered record with the documented handover. “This supply lead and this payment lead need separate work.”
“Shinokami and Syndicate,” Fox said.
“Specific connections. Not every person who works near them.”
“I heard you the first case.”
“I know. I'm writing it for someone who didn't.”
Fox sat, checked a small item of equipment and frowned at it. Gordon moved a loose paper away from his working hand.
“You need room?”
“I need this part to stop catching.”
“Is that a request?”
“It could become one.”
Gordon waited. Fox tried once more, then handed over the part he could safely offer without inventing an equipment mechanic.
Asking for help with something small ought not to feel like admitting a larger weakness. He disliked noticing that it sometimes did.
He resisted making the request significant by acknowledging it too warmly. Fox had asked for a practical contribution. Gordon made it.

They returned to the file when the ordinary interruption was finished. The worker’s limited account remained limited; the courier’s materials opened the next lines. A wider investigation did not make the people who had helped into secret experts.

FD10.title: The account they can give
FD10.chapter: Chapter 4 — The witness is not the bait

elements.text: The contractor stopped at the date.
“I thought it was before that.”
Fox looked at the referral. “You thought, or you remember?”
The contractor's hands moved away from the paper.
“I remember going. I can't make the date arrive because you keep looking at me.”
Gordon let the sentence finish.
“We can take a pause,” he said.
“I want to get this over with.”
“Then let's separate the date on the document from the date you were there.”

They compared the original fields, the delivery manifest and the existing exterior observations. The processing date was not the physical visit date. That clarified the apparent discrepancy; it did not explain every uncertainty in the account.
Fox asked a narrower question about the portion the contractor had personally seen.
“This part,” the contractor said, touching the page. “I can tell you that.”
At the frontage, away from the witness, Fox spoke quietly.
“You didn't like the question.”
“I didn't like it becoming a demand to remember faster.”
“And if the gap was deliberate?”
“We test what we can. Immediate protection doesn't depend on a perfect account.”

He wanted Gordon to acknowledge that uncomfortable questions could still be necessary. He had also seen the person withdraw from the paper, and could not pretend tone had no effect simply because his suspicion was possible.
He wanted to protect the interview from pressure, not protect every statement from examination. It mattered to say the difference instead of assuming Fox would hear it in his patience.
“The date check helped,” Gordon said.
Fox looked back toward the verified frontage. “Next question can be smaller.”

FD11.title: Pursuit or protection
FD11.chapter: Chapter 4 — The witness is not the bait

elements.text: Before the actual protection encounter, they reviewed the current threat and their available positions. The contractor would not be used to keep an opponent interested while they chased a more exciting lead.
“If someone moves beyond the frontage?” Fox asked.
“We assess what we can cover without abandoning the witness.”
Fox glanced at him. “We've had this conversation.”
“Yes,” Gordon said. “Let's have it before the choice this time.”
The old argument returned with uncomfortable precision.

FM03.title: The trail they did not follow
FM03.chapter: Chapter 4 — The witness is not the bait

elements.text: FLASHBACK — A later early-partnership incident; date unspecified
A potentially relevant carrier was moving away. The available positions did not let the pair pursue safely while protecting the consenting witness from an immediate, visible threat.
Fox began tracking the route with his attention.
“Fox. Back here,” Gordon called.
Fox looked between the two problems. He returned. The witness was protected and the carrier got away. Neither later learned what that lost lead would have proved.
The argument came after the urgent work, not while the witness was waiting to be helped.
“You asked me to watch the route,” Fox said. “Then you asked me to let it go.”
“Yes. I needed you back.”
“Then say that. Don't tell me it stopped mattering.”
“It mattered. I chose the person we could still reach.”
Fox turned away, then turned back.
“And whoever that carrier reaches next?”
“We don't know what they were carrying.”
“We won't know now.”
“No,” Gordon said. “We won't.”
That answer stopped the argument for a moment without ending it.

He had wanted Gordon to insist the lead was worthless, because that would have been easier to fight. Instead Gordon acknowledged the loss. Fox still resented how little explanation had accompanied the call, and was no longer sure what to do with the resentment.

He wanted the successful protection to settle the decision. It did not settle what Fox had been asked to abandon or the way the request had been made. He could defend the priority without pretending the cost was imaginary.
“I need to know you'll come when someone is exposed,” Gordon said.
“I came.”
“Yes. You did.”
“Don't argue with the version where I didn't.”
Gordon took a breath. “Fair.”
Fox waited.
“I can explain the change when there's time,” Gordon said. “When there isn't, I still need the response. Then we talk about the decision afterward.”
“And if I think you're wrong?”
“Say it when we can actually discuss it.”
Fox did not offer a broad promise that any order would be right. “Tell me what you need, not that the thing I was doing never mattered.”
Gordon nodded.

They left without pretending to have reached identical conclusions. On the next collaboration, Gordon explained the changing priority as soon as he could. Fox announced a proposed move before leaving his position. Those actions did more than the last sentence of the argument had.
PRESENT DAY
They divided observation and protection for the contractor case. Agreeing where to stand did not make either of them invulnerable.

FD12.title: Four desks, no names
FD12.chapter: Chapter 4 — The witness is not the bait

elements.text: After the successful protection, they checked the contractor’s permitted account once more.
Gordon checked what remained essential. “We need to confirm this part. Then we can use the account you've already given instead of asking you to start again.”
Fox moved the material within their reach, not beneath their hand.
At the briefing, four coded desks appeared on the verified record. The names behind them were not yet established.
“Four,” Fox said.
“Four independent enquiries.”
“You make that sound manageable.”
“I make it sound separate.”
Fox studied the document. “Somebody put them together.”
“Yes. We establish each connection before deciding how.”

The case had widened faster than the street had become safer. He could feel the attraction of a single explanation, something that would turn all the scattered harm into one target. He did not yet say that aloud.

Dividing the work gave him a procedure. It could not give him the certainty that finishing the procedure would make the result controllable. For now there were four specific questions, and he could refuse to mistake that for four answers.
They authorised the four enquiries. Before leaving, Gordon checked the contractor’s follow-up arrangement. Fox waited without treating it as an interruption to the important part.

FD13.title: Whose order
FD13.chapter: Chapter 5 — The escort that changed hands

elements.text: The driver remembered taking the packet.
“I remember being told the loading order had changed.”
“And you passed that on,” Fox said.
“Yes.”
“Who changed it?”
“I didn't write it.”
Gordon placed the archived original beside the working copy. The receiving acknowledgment and the authorising signature occupied different fields.
Fox looked at the driver's initials. “You carried the instruction.”
“I carried a packet. I told people what I was told about the order.”
Gordon turned slightly toward Fox. “Then ask what he carried. Not why he wrote it.”
The driver watched them, silent.
Fox looked back. “What did you personally see?”

The answer was narrower than the theory and useful within that limit. The dispatch record and original authorisation could be compared with the independently witnessed deployment. That established the actual operational linkage; a substitute driver's presence did not establish command.

It was irritating to revise the question in front of somebody who had already begun defending themselves. He did it anyway. Making the interview less comfortable was not the same as making it more accurate.
He had corrected Fox without intending a performance. The driver was still an audience to it. Gordon made sure the next question concerned the record, not his partner's judgement.
After the driver declined further optional conversation, Fox respected the answer.
“Still a connection,” he said outside.
“A witness to part of one.”
Fox nodded. “I know the difference.”
“Then it will be clear in what we write.”
The original order and independently witnessed deployment identified Martos Cabrera as the Ace of Clubs. The conclusion belonged to the assembled investigation team.

FD14.title: Standing between
FD14.chapter: Chapter 5 — The escort that changed hands

elements.text: Martos's lack of haste unsettled him more than a shouted threat would have. Here was someone who looked capable of holding a promise through difficulty. Fox knew exactly why that quality could make an enemy dangerous.

Martos did not appear confused about why they had come. Gordon would not spend the exchange pretending more explanation alone must produce cooperation. He still owed the specific request its clear statement.
“The original order and the deployment establish your role,” Gordon said. “We are here about this operation.”
“Then speak about the operation,” Martos answered.
Fox glanced at the position he held. “You intend to keep us from it.”
“Yes.”
“Stand aside,” Gordon said.
“No.”
The simplicity left a silence neither investigator could fill usefully.
“You understand what we're asking,” Gordon said.
“I do.”
“And this is your answer.”
Martos nodded once.
Fox looked toward his partner. “Then we've reached the part that needs less talking.”

FD15.title: The limits of a victory
FD15.chapter: Chapter 5 — The escort that changed hands

elements.text: Fox sat longer than he usually did before beginning the discussion.
“He knew what he was doing.”
“Yes,” Gordon said.
“No misunderstanding to clear up. No little detail that makes him step aside.”
“That isn't an exemption from what the operation established.”
“I didn't say it was.”
Gordon put down the page. “No. You didn't.”

He had wanted to name the effort it took to get past deliberate loyalty. Gordon had heard the start of an excuse. Fox could see why, and still resented having to explain that respecting competence did not require forgiving its use.

He had moved too quickly from recognition to correction. There were things the case file could state precisely and things a partner needed a minute to say without being mistaken for a defence of the opponent.
“One position,” Fox said. “That much work.”
Gordon nodded. “We remember that before the next one.”

The record included the independently established identity, the victory and the recovered command material. It claimed neither permanent custody nor the destruction of the Suit. Outside the review, both still had the ordinary work of restoring their readiness.
The witness's account became less certain when Gordon asked which part they had seen themselves.
“The coat. The way the person moved. People said it was—”
“Before or after you told them?” Fox asked.
The witness stopped.
“I'm asking when the name entered it,” Fox added. “Not telling you that you made everything up.”

Gordon placed the actual schedule beside the original instruction. They compared the voluntarily supplied call sheet, its timing and the independently observed deployment. A similar costume had made a particular person an easy answer. The times did not support that attribution.

The public account had sounded coherent enough to guide a check. He had to notice where coherence had begun to feel like corroboration. It was not Fox's responsibility to keep him from finding a tidy story attractive.

He distrusted how readily a group could finish one person's uncertainty. That did not mean the witness deserved contempt for having listened to other people. He kept the useful question smaller than his irritation.
“So I got it wrong?” the witness asked.
“This identification isn't supported,” Gordon said. “We can retain what you actually observed and correct the name attached to it.”
“Will everyone hear I lied?”
“We aren't recording a lie we haven't established.”

They corrected the attribution with the people they had interviewed. The original instruction and independently observed masked deployment identified Elias Braun as the Ace of Hearts. The finding stayed in the team’s record.
Elias looked between the two investigators before addressing Gordon.
“You have already decided how this conversation ends.”
“We decided which records match. Your response is still yours.”
“And he has come to provide the punctuation?”
Fox's answer was immediate. “I can speak for myself.”
Gordon did not step into the space Fox had claimed. “Then answer both of us.”
He disliked how quickly the remark had found something worth defending. He was not here to persuade Elias that he had a mind. He could use it by returning to the instruction they had actually traced.
The temptation was to announce the partnership in a reassuring sentence. It would have made him the person explaining Fox again. He let his partner ask the next question.
“The instruction reached the people who carried it out,” Fox said. “What part are you disputing?”
“That a document tells you everything about the person holding it.”
“It doesn't have to tell us everything,” Gordon said.
Elias's smile changed, without disappearing entirely.
“You're very careful.”
“We corrected a wrong identification,” Gordon said. “We aren't replacing it with another assumption.”
“Then you know what you're asking me to accept.”
“Yes.”
Elias had refused the operation’s request. The conversation had reached its limit; the encounter ahead remained unresolved.
Fox put distance between himself and the confrontation before speaking again.
“He wanted me to prove I wasn't what he called me.”
Gordon waited.
“And I almost wasted the whole conversation doing it.”
“You asked about the instruction.”
“Eventually.”
Gordon considered that. “I could have spent just as long answering every objection.”
“You like a well-phrased objection.”
“I prefer one with a relevant answer.”
Fox gave him a dry look. “Dangerous hobby.”
The joke made it easier to admit the anger without pretending it had been a brilliant tactic. He had regained the useful question. That was worth remembering more than the insult.

He could acknowledge his own attraction to the exchange without turning it into a competition over who had been more susceptible. The room had been arranged rhetorically as well as physically, and they had both had to find their way through it.

They returned to the case record. The wrongly attributed performer remained excluded by the actual checks. Defeating Elias did not make the earlier public rumour retrospectively accurate or its witnesses dishonest.
The routine payment was genuine. Gordon checked the original record again before setting it beside the disputed authorisation.
“It may explain the shared label.”
Fox leaned closer. “May.”
“Yes.”
“You sound relieved.”
“I would be pleased to exclude a wrong inference.”
“That isn't quite what I said.”

They compared the service period, amount, recipient and approval authority. A willing accounts worker explained the process they actually operated and declined to speculate about decisions outside it.
The shared trading label was not the whole recipient chain. The routine invoice concerned different work. Its authenticity did not explain the separate authorisation.
“This payment is genuine,” Gordon said.
“That doesn't make it the payment we're asking about,” Fox replied.
“I know that now.”
Fox stopped preparing his next point.

He had wanted the less dramatic explanation to work. That was not inherently a fault, but it could become one if he treated complexity as evidence against the remaining concern. He recorded why the explanation was insufficient rather than merely discarding it.

He had distrusted the tidy answer before checking it, which was not the same as disproving it. The comparison had done useful work even though it had brought them back to suspicion. He could admit that without congratulating the paperwork.
“It had to be checked,” Fox said.
Gordon nodded. “Yes.”
The independent originals identified Camila Lopez as the Ace of Diamonds. The accounts worker had explained a process, not confessed to a conspiracy. The routine invoice remained genuine.
Camila listened to the stated finding without interrupting.
“You have established my involvement,” she said. “What else do you think that establishes?”
“The authorisation in this file,” Gordon answered. “Not every decision made by the organisation.”
“Good. Keep that distinction when you lose patience.”
Fox looked at her. “Keep it when you run out of objections.”
“I haven't disputed your finding.”
“Will you cooperate with the operation?” Gordon asked.
“You have mistaken agreement about a fact for agreement about what follows.”
“No,” Fox said. “We're asking.”
She looked between them. The narrow acknowledgment did not make her their source or change her allegiance.

Her insistence on precision resembled a discipline he valued. He could respect the distinction without allowing it to turn an operational refusal into an endless discussion. He had asked a question with an actual consequence attached.

Camila gave Gordon plenty to answer. Fox could feel the discussion growing another branch whenever one had been dealt with. He wanted the refusal stated plainly, not because he disliked thinking, but because they still had to act on what was no longer uncertain.
Gordon read one paragraph twice. Fox noticed.
“You going to revise it by staring?”
“I was considering a sentence.”
“For quite a while.”
Gordon put the page down. “Fine. We can stop for a moment.”
Fox pushed a chair into a more usable position. “Didn't ask for permission.”
“No. You issued an observation.”
“A useful one.”

Gordon almost smiled. They checked the equipment that actually needed attention. When Fox asked him to hold something steady, Gordon did not turn the request into an opportunity to discuss accepting help.

The quiet was easier when their hands had something ordinary to do. He could notice Gordon's fatigue without asking for an explanation of it, and could accept assistance without promising it meant something larger.

He had spent the confrontation trying not to let a precise objection take over the whole room. He had then almost done the same thing with his own report. Fox's blunt interruption had been annoying and timely.
After a while Gordon said, “She revised quickly.”
“Still lost the encounter.”
“Yes. Both are worth recording.”
Fox nodded. They finished the practical task before returning to the files. Neither pretended a short rest had made the work effortless.

FD22.title: More than one trail
FD22.chapter: Chapter 8 — A trace through the crowd

elements.text: Fox reported the trace on the shared handover surface and the apparent route beyond it.
“How continuous?” Gordon asked.
Fox's answer came slowly. “Present. I didn't say continuous.”
“You pointed along the route.”
“I was showing you where it appears.”
They looked at each other for a moment, each hearing a larger accusation than the other had actually made.
Gordon spoke first. “I'm asking what can be inferred from it.”
“Not whether I sensed it.”
“No.”

They compared accessible contact surfaces and the documented handover time. A shared handling item had moved between locations; a dated service record and a willing observer corroborated that movement. The trace could travel without proving the same person's continuous journey.

It was a relief to have a physical explanation and an irritation to need it. He was accustomed to being certain that he had perceived something. The harder discipline was deciding how much of the world that certainty actually described.
He could hear Fox distinguishing the limit more carefully now. Gordon needed to leave space for that correction rather than reward it with a lecture about what he had been asking all along.
“Transferred,” Fox said. “No continuous route established.”
“Deliberately?”
“Nothing here proves that.”
Gordon nodded and recorded the distinction.

The independently documented handover and witnessed operational encounter remained the valid route to Mavis's chosen operational identity. No legal name appeared from a scent, and no trap was invented simply because an inference had failed.

FD23.title: The person behind the mask
FD23.chapter: Chapter 8 — A trace through the crowd

elements.text: Mavis waited at the confrontation point and let Gordon state the finding. Her stillness left Fox watching more carefully, not seeing more than was there.
“The handover and the operational encounter identify you as the Ace of Spades.”
“Then use that name.”
Fox looked at her. “We're here about what happened here.”
“Keep it there.”
Gordon did not ask for a birth name to make the exchange sound complete.

Her few words left room for him to hear everything he wanted in them. He resisted. Privacy was not itself a threat, and her reserve did not establish knowledge of the misleading trace they had already rejected.

The urge to make an identification feel final could be stronger than the evidence. Their record connected a chosen name to an operational role. He would not pretend the file contained a person in full.
“You followed something,” Mavis said.
“Several things,” Fox answered. “I checked which ones belonged together.”
“Keep doing that.”
“Will you stand aside for the operation?” Gordon asked.
“No.”
The answer stayed plain. She did not become a riddle or a reluctant informant because they had respected the limits of the case.

FD24.title: What we can connect
FD24.chapter: Chapter 8 — A trace through the crowd

elements.text: Fox watched Gordon enter the actual result.
“For a while I didn't have a clean picture,” he said.
“You told me.”
“I'm used to having something better than that to give you.”
Gordon stopped writing. “Knowing you couldn't confirm a position was useful.”
“Doesn't feel like much.”
“It kept me from acting as though you had.”
Fox looked down at the table. He did not answer immediately.

He wanted his usefulness to be something he could hand over whole. Gordon was describing a contribution made out of a limit. It would take time for that to feel like anything but an absence, but he could understand why it mattered.
He did not need to praise Fox into accepting the point. The next plan would demonstrate whether he actually valued the admission. He returned to the file and kept the wording accurate.

“This one is complete,” Gordon said.

“Then we look at the next one as its own problem,” Fox answered. The other enquiries still had their own questions to answer.

Gordon laid the four recovered command records together. Fox stood to see them.

“Now we can ask what connects them.”

Gordon nodded. “Now. Not before.”

FD25.title: Four records, one pattern
